documents: The study included the synthetic small molecule ligand MDL-29951, which was used to reveal the competitive antagonism of RWT020016.
The study characterized GPR17 expression in postmortem human brain and optic nerve tissue using a bioinformatics approach with single-nucleus RNA sequencing data.
Efficacy of the GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 was examined in toxin-induced demyelination mouse models using both acute and chronic cuprizone treatment.
Functional and behavioral readouts in the mouse models included visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and a Y-maze test assessing spatial working memory.

Structural readouts in the mouse models included quantification of myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum and assessment of myelin ultrastructure via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in the optic nerve.
The study included MDL-29951 to reveal a competitive antagonism of RWT020016.
The study utilized postmortem immunohistochemical analyses of multiple sclerosis patient tissue to evaluate GPR17 expression.
The study evaluated the effects of a novel, selective GPR17 antagonist in cuprizone-induced murine demyelination models.

The cuprizone-induced murine demyelination models were selected because they allow for the study of de- and remyelination mechanisms in the absence of the full inflammatory complexity of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis.
The murine subjects received oral treatment with the GPR17 antagonist.
Functional recovery was assessed by measuring improved spatial memory and recovery of visual evoked potential latency delays.
Structural remyelination was assessed in the corpus callosum and optic nerve.

Five public single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets were collected, yielding a total of 214,567 nuclei, and were processed using the Seurat R package version 3.1 with a consistent quality control pipeline that excluded low-quality nuclei based on low gene counts or high mitochondrial transcript content.

Datasets were integrated using the Seurat integration workflow to mitigate batch effects, followed by dimensionality reduction via principal component analysis with 7,500 variable features and 75 principal components retained, and cell embedding using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP).

Clustering was performed using a graph-based approach with FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions, and marker genes were identified using Seurat's FindAllMarkers function with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, resulting in a final subsetted dataset of 71,623 oligodendrocyte lineage cells.

Brightfield images of 3,3-diaminobenzidine (DAB)-stained sections were acquired using an Axio Scan Z.1 microscope (Zeiss) equipped with Neoplanfluor objectives to capture entire multiple sclerosis lesions. These images were recorded with an Evolution MP camera (Media Cybernetics) and processed using ImagePro software.

Fluorescent images were obtained using an Axio Scan Z.1 (Zeiss) with a Plan-Apochromat 20x/0.8 M27 objective. An Evolution black-and-white camera (MediaCybernetics) and ImagePro software (MediaCybernetics) were used for image capture and analysis, respectively.

For the qualitative assessment, a total of 3-4 sections per tissue block were included, and all visibly distinct lesions (2-6 per section) were evaluated separately. This assessment covered all visibly distinct lesions for each donor and tissue block dissected, specifically from the neocortex and optic nerves.

The test compound RWT020016 was synthesized by the CRO Pharmaron Inc. via standard solution-phase synthesis from commercially available building blocks using established coupling, substitution, and protection-deprotection strategies. The synthesis was followed by chromatographic purification and routine analytical characterization.

Human brain tissues and optic nerves from eight donors diagnosed with primary or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (two men and six women) were obtained from the Netherlands Brain Bank for qualitative immunohistochemical analyses. The sample acquisition period spanned from 01.01.1996 to 31.12.2018, and all analyses were conducted at the Netherlands Brain Bank using anonymized donor clinical records.

The use of brain autoptic samples and procedures was approved by the Ethics Committee of Amsterdam UMC (Location VUmc, Amsterdam, The Netherlands), which is registered with the U.S. Office of Human Research Protections under IRB number IRB00002991 and Federal-wide Assurance number 00003703.

Double immunostaining was performed on sections from all dissected tissue blocks to visualize proteolipid protein (PLP) and human leukocyte antigen (HLA-DR-DQ) for the classification of demyelinating lesions.

The eight multiple sclerosis donors included in the study had postmortem delays ranging from 07:00 to 10:40 hours, cerebrospinal fluid pH levels between 6.1 and 7.2, and brain weights between 998 and 1390 grams. Tissue fixation methods varied among formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) and cryo sections, with specific tissue types including cerebral cortex lesions, optic nerves, and the optic chiasm.
Coronal sections 8 μm thick were cut from cryotissue using a cryostat and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate-buffered saline (1x PBS, pH 7.6).
Cryosections were incubated overnight at 4°C in a blocking solution containing 10% normal horse serum, 1% bovine serum albumin, and 0.5% Triton X-100 in 1x PBS along with primary antibodies.
Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections were deparaffinized and processed for antigen retrieval in 10 mM Citrate buffer pH 6.0 for GPR17 or 1x TBS pH 7.6 for HLA and PLP.

The study used mouse anti-human HLA-DP, DQ, DR antigen (DAKO, M077501-2) at a dilution of 1:100 for FFPE and 1:500 for cryotissue, and mouse anti-PLP (Bio-Rad, MCA839G) at 1:500 for FFPE and 1:6000 for cryotissue.

The study utilized rabbit anti-GPR17 (Sigma-Aldrich, HPA026) at a 1:100 dilution for both FFPE and cryotissue, and mouse anti-BCAS1 clone 5 (Santa Cruz, sc-136342) at a 1:10,000 dilution for both tissue types.

The NeuroPK experiments utilized SPF-grade male C57/BL6J mice obtained from Zhejiang Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd. (license number: SCXK (浙) 2020-0002) and were maintained under a reverse 12-hour light/dark cycle at 21-22°C with ad libitum access to food and water.

Cuprizone-induced demyelination was induced by feeding mice a pelleted diet containing 0.3% (w/w) cuprizone (Bis(cyclohexanone)oxaldihydrazone; Sigma-Aldrich, C9012-25G) formulated by Bio-Services/Sniff for either 6 weeks (acute model) or 12 weeks (chronic model).

Compound or vehicle treatment began 2 days before the cessation of cuprizone feeding to ensure sufficient brain exposure at the onset of the remyelination phase, a timing choice based on previous pilot studies indicating robust treatment effects.
Animals were euthanized with pentobarbital at a dose of 200 mg/kg administered intraperitoneally at the study end or if the humane-endpoint threshold of 30% weight loss was reached.

Single-dose pharmacokinetic studies and brain exposure analyses for RWT020016 were performed by the CRO Pharmaron Inc. using standard industry NeuroPK protocols with N=3 animals and a dose volume of 5 ml/kg.
Plasma samples were obtained by terminal cardiac puncture, while brain tissues were collected following exsanguination and saline perfusion to minimize residual blood contamination.
Plasma and brain homogenate concentrations were quantified using a validated LC-MS/MS method, and pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated using noncompartmental analysis.

cAMP accumulation assays were performed by the CRO Eurofins DiscoverX using CHO-K1 cells stably expressing the recombinant murine GPR17 receptor, with dose-response curves for RWT020016 generated at eight concentrations, each tested in duplicate.

For antagonist testing, cells were preincubated with RWT020016 for 10 min, followed by the addition of a mixture containing forskolin (1 μM) and the GPR17 agonist MDL-29951 (EC80, 200 nM), then incubated for 30 min at room temperature.

Lysis buffer containing cAMP-d2 and anti-cAMP cryptate detection reagent (Cisbio #62AM4PEJ) was added, and plates were incubated for 1 h at room temperature before measuring fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) ratios using the HTRF kit.

Calcium mobilization-based potency and selectivity assays were performed by the CRO Axxam S.p.A. using the Fluorescence Imaging Plate Reader FLIPR TETRA ICCD camera (Molecular Devices) and automated liquid handling systems including the Hamilton Microlab STAR (Hamilton) and CyBio Felix and CyBio Well Vario systems (CyBio).

For potency assessment, HEK293 cells stably expressing either the murine or human short GPR17 isoform were loaded with 20 μL per well of 0.5× calcium-sensitive dye (Fluo-8 NW; AAT Bioquest) in Tyrode's buffer and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C.

Cells in the potency assessment were treated with RWT020016 in a dose-response format for 20 min, then stimulated with the selective GPR17 agonist MDL-29951 at an EC80 concentration of 200 nM, with vehicle-treated cells serving as controls.

For selectivity testing, human P2Y1, P2Y2, and P2Y11 receptors were transiently expressed in 1321N1 cells, and human CysLTR1 was transiently expressed in HEK293 cells, with corresponding wild-type cell lines serving as negative controls.

Cells in the selectivity testing were loaded with Fluo-8 NW dye, treated with RWT020016 in a dose-response format for 20 min, and stimulated with reference agonists at EC80 concentrations (ATP for P2Y receptors, LTD4 for CysLTR1).

Additional control conditions in the selectivity testing included treatment with reference antagonists MRS2500 (P2Y1), ARC-118925 XX (P2Y2), Suramin (P2Y11), and Pranlukast (CysLTR1) in a dose-response format, followed by stimulation with the corresponding reference agonists.
Fluorescence signals were recorded in real time, and data were analyzed using Genedata Screener® software (Genedata AG) and expressed as a percentage effect relative to normalization standards.

Cuprizone experiments were conducted at the Hasselt University animal facility using nine-week-old male C57BL/6OlaHsd mice (Envigo/Inotiv) that were single housed under standard enriched conditions with ad libitum access to food and water, controlled temperature (21-22°C), and an inverted light cycle.

Mice were treated once daily via oral gavage (10 µl/g body weight) for 9 days in the acute model or 37 days in the chronic model with the selective GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 dissolved in a vehicle of 1% (v/v) DMSO, 0.5% (w/v) methylcellulose (M0512, Sigma-Aldrich), and 2% (v/v) Tween 80 (P1754, Sigma-Aldrich) at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg.

Spatial working memory was assessed using the spontaneous Y-maze alternation task at the end of demyelination (week 6 and week 12) and remyelination (week 7 and week 17) in the acute and chronic cuprizone models, respectively, where each mouse explored three arms for 6 minutes and an arm entry was recorded when both hind paws fully entered an arm.

The primary measure of spatial working memory was the percentage of spontaneous alternation, calculated as (Number of correct triads / (total arm entries - 2)) × 100, with a correct triad defined as a sequence of consecutive entries into three different arms.

Data were analyzed by an experimenter blinded to treatment groups for the initial 2-minute trial in the acute cuprizone model and the entire 6-minute trial in the chronic cuprizone model, and mice that failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial were excluded from analysis due to insufficient exploration.

Mouse optic nerves were fixed at week 17 of the chronic cuprizone study following a lethal injection of 200 mg/kg pentobarbital and cardiac perfusion, then immersed overnight at 4°C in 2% glutaraldehyde in 0.05 M sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 7.3).

The optic nerves were post-fixed in 2% osmium tetroxide in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer for 60 minutes, dehydrated through ascending ethanol concentrations, incubated in propylene oxide for 60 minutes, and infiltrated with a 1:1 propylene oxide and epoxy resin mixture before being embedded in Epon and polymerized at 60°C for 48 hours.

Ultrathin cross-sections of 60-80 nm were cut on a Reichert Ultracut microtome, mounted on copper grids, and stained with lead citrate prior to image acquisition using transmission electron microscopy (TEM).

Five randomly selected and blinded images of optic nerve sections per mouse were analyzed using Fiji ImageJ software to calculate the g-ratio as the inner axonal diameter divided by the total outer diameter of the myelinated fiber.
G-ratios were measured for 25 axons per image to assess myelin thickness, and ultrastructural pathology was evaluated using a semi-quantitative TEM-based scoring system.

A pilot study assessed the numerical density of axons containing mitochondria within five images of 200 μm² size per animal (n=5), yielding an average of 0.15/μm² which served as the reference for normal mitochondrial density and morphology in the current study.

The study used a cumulative pathology scoring system where a baseline score of 0 was assigned for the absence of pathological features, and +1 was added for each of six specific ultrastructural hallmarks: altered mitochondrial morphology, loose myelin sheaths, empty or swollen axons, degenerating axons with debris, fully degenerated axons with only myelin debris, and enlarged periaxonal space.

Samples were classified into four grades based on the average score per optic nerve: grade 1 (score 2-3, none), grade 2 (score 3-4, mild), grade 3 (score 4-5, moderate), and grade 4 (score 5-6, severe).

All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism for Windows version 10.2.1, with data presented as mean values ± standard error of the mean (SEM) and differences considered statistically significant at p<0.05.
Mice that failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial were excluded from analysis due to insufficient exploration.

Visual evoked potential (VEP) recordings were performed at baseline, week 6, and week 7 in the acute model, and at week 12 and week 17 in the chronic model, with mice dark-adapted overnight prior to testing.
Anesthesia for VEP recordings was induced via intraperitoneal injection of 5 µl/g body weight of xylazine (10 mg/kg) and ketamine (70 mg/kg) dissolved in saline.
Pupillary dilation for VEP recordings was achieved using 0.5% tropicamide followed by 10% phenylephrine.

The electrophysiological setup for VEP recordings used a subdermal recording electrode over the visual cortex, a reference electrode in the tongue, and a ground electrode at the base of the tail, with impedance measurements confirming connectivity.
Each mouse was exposed to 200 white light flashes of 310 ms duration at 1 Hz frequency and 0.5 cd·s/m² intensity for VEP recording.
VEP recordings were performed in complete darkness inside a Faraday cage using the CELERIS system (Diagnosys), and data were analyzed using Diagnosys ESPION software (Diagnosys).
VEP traces were analyzed offline by an experimenter blinded to treatment groups, with values from both eyes of each mouse averaged for statistical analysis.
Mice were perfused intracardially with saline after a 200 mg/kg pentobarbital intraperitoneal injection, and brains were post-fixed overnight in 4% PFA.
Brain sections were incubated in a graded sucrose series (10%, 20%, and 30%), embedded in optimal cutting temperature medium, and coronal cryosections of 5 µm were prepared at Bregma -2.0 mm.
Cryosections were fixed in ice-cold acetone and incubated with blocking buffer (0.05% Triton X-100 and 10% DAKO protein block in PBS) before overnight incubation with primary antibodies.
Primary antibodies used were rat anti-myelin basic protein (MAB386, Millipore, 1:500) or rabbit anti-GPR17 (10136, Sanbio Cayman Chemicals, 1:200), diluted in blocking buffer.
Secondary antibodies were anti-rat Alexa 555 (A21434, Life Technologies, 1:400) or anti-rabbit Alexa 555 (A31572, Life Technologies, 1:400), diluted in 1x PBS.
DAPI was used to counterstain cell nuclei, and slides were mounted using Fluoromount G (00-4958-02, Life Technologies).
Representative high-resolution images of MBP- and GPR17-stained sections were acquired with a Leica DM2000 LED fluorescence microscope.
Immunoreactivity was quantified using a densitometric method with a binary threshold applied via the default ImageJ (Fiji) thresholding plugin in a 32-image format.
The area above threshold within a fixed-dimension square region of interest in the medial corpus callosum at Bregma -2.0 mm was measured to calculate the percentage area stained.
All immunohistochemistry analyses were performed blinded, and values from the cuprizone and treatment groups were expressed relative to the control group.

Brain and optic nerve sections were stained for proteolipid protein (PLP) to visualize myelin and for GPR17 to localize GPR17-expressing cells, with high-resolution imaging using co-staining for BCAS1 and DAPI.

Lesions were classified according to a standard MS lesion scoring system with codes 0-6, and no formal quantitative comparisons across lesion types were performed due to limited sample numbers and inter-patient heterogeneity.
Single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis included a total of 214,567 cells, with a specific population of 71,623 cells of the oligodendrocyte lineage combined from five human brain studies.

The study utilized sample-based integration of non-neuronal cells to minimize dataset- and sample-specific variation, which enabled the delineation of the rare and transient population of committed oligodendrocyte precursors (COPs).

Cluster identities in the single-nucleus transcriptomic data were validated using canonical marker genes for microglia (FYB1, C3), astrocytes (AQP4, GJA1), oligodendrocytes (MOBP, MBP), neurons (GRIN1, GAD2, SLC17A7), and endothelial cells (CLDN5).

Lesions in the brain and optic nerve sections were classified according to established histopathological criteria published by Luchetti et al. based on demyelination status and microglia/macrophage activity.

Brain and optic nerve sections were stained for GPR17, HLA/PLP, and BCAS1 (Brain Enriched Myelin Associated Protein 1) to investigate the spatial relationship between GPR17 expression and multiple sclerosis lesion pathology.

The selectivity profile of RWT020016 was evaluated against cysteinyl leukotriene receptors (hCYSLTR1) and purinergic P2Y family members (P2Y1, P2Y2, P2Y11) at concentrations up to 50 µM, where RWT020016 showed no measurable activity.
RWT020016 was profiled using the CEREP SafetyScreen87 panel from Eurofins at a dose of 10 µM to identify off-target drug activity across 87 molecular targets.

Follow-on functional studies at Eurofins determined that RWT020016 exhibits low micromolar antagonistic activity at the 5-HT2A receptor with an IC50 of 4 µM and low agonistic activity at the KOR with an EC50 of 9.9 µM.

Pharmacokinetic studies of RWT020016 were conducted after single oral administration at 3 mg/kg in C57BL/6 mice, revealing a bioavailability of 91% and peak plasma concentrations (Cmax) exceeding 12,000 ng/mL.

The study utilized acute (0.3% cuprizone for 6 weeks) and chronic (0.3% cuprizone for 12 weeks) cuprizone models, with animals returned to normal placebo pellets for 1 week and 5 weeks respectively to allow spontaneous remyelination. Compound treatment was initiated two days prior to cuprizone withdrawal to ensure sufficient compound concentration in the brain to initiate remyelination.

Visual evoked potential (VEP) latency and amplitude were assessed at baseline, at the end of the demyelination phase (week 6 for acute, week 12 for chronic), and at the end of the remyelination phase (week 7 for acute, week 17 for chronic). VEPs were used to assess the functional integrity of the visual pathways, where latency prolongation indicates slowed conduction and amplitude reduction indicates axonal injury.

Mice were subjected to the Y-maze spontaneous alternation test at the end of the demyelination phase to evaluate cognitive processing speed and episodic memory. General locomotor activity was investigated by measuring total arm entries to rule out confounding effects on cognitive performance.

Structural changes in myelin following acute and chronic cuprizone exposure were investigated by evaluating myelin basic protein (MBP) immunohistochemical expression in the medial corpus callosum. Quantitative analysis of MBP expression was performed to confirm the loss of myelin induced by cuprizone.

Functional demyelination was evaluated by measuring visual evoked potential (VEP) latency at the end of the demyelination phase, using a Two-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test with sample sizes of N=10 for the acute model and N=5-10 for the chronic model.

The total number of entries in the spontaneous alternation Y-maze test was performed at the end of the demyelination phase with sample sizes of N=11 for the acute model and N=10-11 for the chronic model, using an unpaired t-test for statistical comparison.

The percentage of spontaneous alternations in the Y-maze was assessed at week 6 for the acute model and week 12 for the chronic model, analyzed via a one-sample t-test against a hypothetical 50% alternation rate with sample sizes of N=10-11.

Myelin basic protein (MBP)-positive area in the medial corpus callosum was quantified following acute and chronic cuprizone demyelination, with statistical significance determined by an unpaired t-test using sample sizes of N=5-10.

Immunohistochemical analysis of GPR17 expression was performed in the medial corpus callosum, followed by quantitative morphometric analysis to confirm upregulation, with statistical comparisons made against control groups using p-values of 0.01 for the acute model and <0.0001 for the chronic model.

The potency of RWT020016 was assessed in cAMP accumulation assays across species and GPR17 isoforms in the presence of the synthetic agonist MDL-29951, yielding an IC50 of 21 nM for human short isoform (s-GPR17), 34 nM for human long isoform (l-GPR17), and 225 nM for murine GPR17.

RWT020016 potency was also measured in a calcium mobilization assay, showing IC50 values between 60 and 75 nM for human s-GPR17 Gai and Gaq signaling pathways, and 142 nM for the murine GPR17 receptor.

RWT020016 potency was measured using calcium mobilization assays and cAMP assays against human and mouse GPR17 receptors, including human short-GPR17 and long-GPR17 isoforms coupled to Gai or Gaq proteins.

The selectivity of RWT020016 was evaluated against closely related Class A GPCRs, including human cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 and human purinergic receptors P2Y1, P2Y2, and P2Y11, using calcium mobilization assays for both antagonism and agonism.

In vivo pharmacokinetic parameters for RWT020016 were determined after single-dose oral administration at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg, with brain-specific metrics including Tmax,brain, Cmax,brain, and AUC0-24h,brain.

The study utilized an in vivo cuprizone model to measure RWT020016 levels in the brain 2 hours after dosing, with average concentrations of 56.6 ng/g (SD=15.8) for the 0.3 mg/kg dose and 232.2 ng/g (SD=89.5) for the 1 mg/kg dose.

GPR17 expression was quantified in the corpus callosum of control and cuprizone-treated mice using an acute model involving 6 weeks of cuprizone treatment and a chronic model involving 12 weeks of demyelination.

Quantification of relative GPR17 protein expression in the corpus callosum used an unpaired t-test with sample sizes of N=9-11 for the acute cuprizone model and N=9-11 for the chronic cuprizone model, presenting data as mean ± SEM fold-change relative to a control mean set to 1.0.

The pharmacokinetic profile of RWT020016 was assessed after single oral administration in mice at doses of 0.3 and 1 mg/kg, with brain exposure time course measurements taken at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours, using N=3 mice per time point.

Functional recovery was assessed by measuring VEP latency following acute and chronic cuprizone-induced demyelination, where the acute model involved 6 weeks of cuprizone treatment followed by one week of recovery, and the chronic model involved 12 weeks of cuprizone treatment followed by 35 days of daily oral dosing of 1 mg/kg RWT020016.
The impact of RWT020016 on spatial working memory was assessed in both acute and chronic cuprizone models, with the acute model evaluated at week 7 and the chronic model evaluated at week 17.

Visual evoked potential (VEP) latency was quantified using a One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test per timepoint, with sample sizes of N=10-11 for both the acute and chronic cuprizone models.
Working memory performance and total arm entries were analyzed using a One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, with sample sizes of N=9-11 for the acute and chronic cuprizone models.
Spontaneous alternation percentages were compared against a hypothetical 50% chance level using a one-sample t-test, with sample sizes of N=9-11.
Myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum was assessed by immunofluorescence staining at week 7 for the acute cuprizone model and week 17 for the chronic cuprizone model.
Quantitative analysis of MBP protein expression was performed using One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, with sample sizes of N=10-11 per group.
RWT020016 was administered at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg to evaluate its effect on MBP protein expression relative to vehicle-treated and control groups.
Data are presented as mean ± SEM relative to the control mean, with mean control values set to 100%.

A semi-quantitative transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis was performed on the optic nerve in the chronic cuprizone model to assess structural changes, specifically analyzing the g-ratio and qualitative morphological features such as mitochondria morphology, myelin integrity, and axon degeneration.

The TEM analysis utilized a small sample size, which the authors note may have contributed to the lack of statistical significance in the g-ratio difference between cuprizone + vehicle mice and naïve controls.
The study utilized RWT0202016, an orally active, potent, selective, and specific GPR17 antagonist, administered at a dose of 1 mg/kg to evaluate its effects on remyelination.
RWT020016 was administered at a dose of 1 mg/kg in cuprizone demyelination mouse models to assess its effect on structural and functional remyelination.

Transmission electron microscopy analysis of the optic nerve involved quantifying G-ratios of 125 axons per optic nerve, measured from five TEM images per optic nerve section, with a sample size of N=6.
The statistical analysis for the G-ratio measurements used a One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, yielding a p-value of 0.049.

Semi-quantitative analysis of optic nerve pathology involved scoring the proportion of none (grade 1), mild (grade 2), moderate (grade 3), and severe (grade 4) pathology with sample sizes ranging from N=6 to N=7.

The study utilized male mice exclusively to reduce biological variability and increase statistical power, a methodological choice that limits the generalizability of the findings regarding sex-dependent differences in pharmacokinetics and remyelination efficacy.

The researchers employed G-ratio analysis and a comprehensive qualitative structural analysis with pathological scoring that integrated mitochondrial morphology, axonal integrity, and myelin integrity to assess axonal repair mechanisms.

The study used cuprizone mouse models to evaluate the therapeutic effects of RWT020016, with structural improvements confirmed by elevated MBP protein levels in the corpus callosum and optic nerve at the ultrastructural level.
The ultrastructural investigations were limited to a small area, and the authors note that histology of optic nerves could strengthen the findings by expanding the analysis to larger tissue sections.
The study leveraged 5 publicly available single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets derived from postmortem human brain to confirm GPR17's selective expression in oligodendrocyte lineage cells.

The authors acknowledge that the relatively small number of available postmortem human samples, combined with substantial inter-patient heterogeneity, variability in lesion size and stage, and differences in tissue preservation and processing, limit the robustness and interpretability of formal quantitative comparisons across lesion types.
Screening assays used cAMP and Ca2+ levels as readouts for downstream signaling events mediated by Gai/o and Gaq proteins to measure the potency of RWT020016.

Electrophysiological assessment was performed using Visual Evoked Potential (VEP) recordings, which were noted to represent a functional surrogate marker of changes along the optic pathway rather than definitive proof of remyelination.

Locomotor activity in the cuprizone model was assessed through total arm entries, a method the authors note lacks additional behavioral controls needed to distinguish working memory performance from anxiety and exploratory behaviour.
Dr. Angelo Quattrini from the Institute of Experimental Neurology, I.R.C.C.S. Ospedale San Raffaelle performed the transmission electron microscopy for the study.
The study combined visual evoked potential (VEP) recording, behavioural assessment, histology, and ultrastructural analysis to evaluate myelin repair.
Single-nucleus RNA sequencing data were visualized using UMAP plots, with gene expression levels represented as log-normalized counts.

The study's reproducibility is compromised because the authors failed to report the exact software versions and parameter settings for the image processing steps in Figure 2, preventing independent verification of whether the low-resolution display is a rendering artifact or a genuine data limitation.

The absence of raw data and specific code for the image processing pipeline means the reported functional gains cannot be independently validated, leaving the entire result dependent on unverified computational parameters that could introduce bias.

With a group size of n=6 or 7, the 95% confidence interval for the primary functional outcome is likely wide enough to encompass the null hypothesis, and the multiple comparisons across secondary structural endpoints significantly inflate the Type I error rate, meaning the claim of 'enhanced recovery' is not supported beyond the uncorrected data.

The study's conclusion that the treatment enhances residual neural function rests on functional metrics rather than verified structural repair, as the lack of access to raw data and processing scripts prevents the definitive exclusion of pipeline artifacts in the image analysis.

The study found that retinal nerve fibre layer thickness was preserved in multiple sclerosis patients compared with controls, while disability scores showed moderate correlations with upper and lower limb functional tests.
Numerous studies utilizing OCT have reported increased Macrophage-like cell (MLC) number, density, and size in various ocular conditions.
Carreño et al. observed an increased number and size of Macrophage-like cells (MLCs) in toxoplasmosis-related ischemic areas.
Pichi et al. identified elevated Macrophage-like cell (MLC) counts in active posterior uveitis.
The study design was a cross-sectional observational study involving patients with multiple sclerosis and age-matched healthy controls.
Retinal imaging was acquired using both spectral-domain optical coherence tomography and swept-source optical coherence tomography angiography.
Macrophage-like cells at the vitreoretinal interface were quantified using an automated image-processing pipeline.
Ganglion cell layer and retinal nerve fibre layer thicknesses were measured using standardized segmentation.
Clinical disability was assessed using the Expanded Disability Status Scale, the 9-Hole Peg Test, and the 25-Foot Walk.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging lesion counts were obtained from T1- and T2-weighted sequences.

The study was a cross-sectional design that included 100 consecutive patients diagnosed with multiple sclerosis according to the 2017 McDonald criteria and 51 healthy controls recruited at the Department of Neurology, Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, between March 2024 and October 2024.

Inclusion criteria for multiple sclerosis patients required a diagnosis per the 2017 McDonald criteria, an age between 18 and 60 years, and a brain MRI with or without contrast performed within the past 12 months.

Exclusion criteria for multiple sclerosis patients included ophthalmologic or systemic disorders affecting the retina, conditions compromising retinal scan quality such as cataracts or corneal opacities, a previous history of optic neuritis, and incomplete medical release during enrollment.

Inclusion criteria for healthy controls required an age between 18 and 60 years, normal MRI findings, no history of uveitis or vitreoretinal pathology, and no personal or family history of multiple sclerosis.

Trained neurologists conducted neurological evaluations at the Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi multiple sclerosis clinic to determine the Expanded Disability Status Scale score and collect MS Functional Composite component tests, including the Timed 25 Foot Walk and 9-hole Peg Test.

Spectral-domain OCT images were acquired using a Spectralis OCT device with Glaucoma Module Premium Edition software (Heidelberg Engineering, Germany) and automatically segmented using Heidelberg Eye Explorer v2.5.1 vendor software, with manual corrections applied for segmentation errors. Image quality and segmentation accuracy were evaluated using the OSCAR-IB criteria.

Macrophage-Like Cell visualization was performed using a Plex Elite 9000 SS-OCTA machine operating at 100 kHz, where a trained ophthalmologist obtained six high-quality 6 x 6 mm OCTA scans centered on the fovea for each eye. Scan acceptance criteria required clear focus, minimal artifacts, no significant saccades, proper centration, regular illumination, and a signal strength of seven or higher.

OCTA scans were exported from the superficial capillary plexus (inner limiting membrane) to the inner plexiform layer for processing, and the vitreoretinal interface slab was adjusted to a 3-μm depth (-7 to -10 μm from the inner limiting membrane) to minimize hyperreflectivity from the retinal nerve fiber layer.

Image processing utilized the "Register Virtual Stack Slices" plugin in FIJI (ImageJ) for elastic registration of six OCTA images, followed by averaging with the "AvgNoiseRmvr" plugin to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio. The same transformation matrix was applied to en-face OCT slabs, which were also averaged to increase the signal-to-noise ratio.

Fast Fourier transform (FFT) filtering and automatic brightness thresholding were applied to highlight MLCs, with particles visually marked in red. The "Analyze Particles" filter was used to measure MLC size, excluding particles smaller than 576 μm², larger than 4896 μm², or with a circularity <0.5.

All measurements were automated using an ImageJ Macro that provided size and count data for further analysis. Morphology-based thresholds were applied to match MLC characteristics during the particle analysis phase.

Independent t-tests were used to analyze continuous variables such as MLC parameters, ganglion cell layer (GCL) thickness, and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness for comparisons between the MS and control groups. A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to assess differences in MLC parameters based on treatment types and disease onset in the MS group.

Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated to explore relationships between EDSS scores and clinical measures such as T1 and T2 lesions, 9-hole Peg Test times, and 25-foot walk times. Correlation analyses were also conducted to evaluate associations between MLC parameters and structural metrics (GCL and RNFL) for both eyes (OD and OS) of MS patients.
Macrophage-like cells (MLC) were identified using an OCTA transform, with background removal and thresholding applied to generate density maps categorized by MLC count.
All statistical analyses were performed using Python with the pandas, scipy, and seaborn libraries, applying a significance threshold of p<0.05.

For correlation analyses between MLC parameters and MRI/clinical variables, the unit of analysis was the individual patient with MLC metrics averaged across both eyes, justified by the moderate-to-strong inter-eye correlation for MLC count (r=0.635, p<0.001).

Bonferroni correction was applied to account for multiple comparisons, setting the adjusted significance threshold to p<0.0083 for the six MLC-MRI correlation analyses and the six regional RNFL comparisons, and to p<0.0125 for the four regional GCL comparisons.

The study included 195 eyes from 100 patients in the MS group and 102 eyes from 51 patients in the control group, with the MS group comprising 91.0% relapsing-remitting, 4.0% secondary progressive, and 2.0% primary progressive phenotypes.
The mean age was 35.08 years (SD=8.67) in the MS group and 35.71 years (SD=9.54) in the control group, with no significant difference in age between the two groups (p=0.69).

The imaging processing pipeline involved averaging 6 consecutive optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) images after registration and averaging en-face OCT images after registration using the OCTA transform.
Macrophage-like cells (MLC) were identified after removing background and applying thresholding to the processed en-face OCT images.

A sensitivity analysis was performed excluding a single data entry outlier with a microglia-like cell (MLC) size of 5843 μm², which was identified in one eye of a patient with an Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score less than 5 and had inflated the mean MLC size in that subgroup.
The statistical comparison for microglia-like cell (MLC) size correlation with T2 lesion burden in multiple sclerosis (MS) patients involved a sample size of n=99.

The study compared ophthalmic parameters, including Best Correct Visual Acuity (BCVA), ganglion cell layer (GCL) thickness, retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) measurements, and macular lacuna (MLC) parameters (count, size, density), between a multiple sclerosis (MS) group and a control group.
The study analyzed correlations between Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores and performance on the 9-Hole Peg Test and 25-foot walk trials in the multiple sclerosis (MS) group.
The study performed a specific comparison of macular lacuna (MLC) parameters between multiple sclerosis (MS) patients with an EDSS score of 5 or more and healthy controls.
The study utilized averaged en-face optical coherence tomography (OCT) at the level of the vitreoretinal interface, specifically analyzing a 3 μm slab.
The study utilized averaged OCT angiography with the added macrophages-like cells (MLC).
The study generated thresholded macrophages-like cells (MLC) images and density maps of MLC.
Retinal mononuclear leukocytes (MLCs) can be visualized in vivo using adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AO-SLO) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA).
Techniques described by Castanos et al. and Uji et al. demonstrated the utility of optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) in tracking hyperreflective cells over time.

The study used ANOVA to analyze MLC parameters across different treatment groups and onset types within the multiple sclerosis cohort. The statistical comparison between relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (n=92) and progressive multiple sclerosis (n=3) was underpowered, so the researchers relied on visual inspection of boxplots instead of statistical testing.

The study used Spearman correlation to assess the association between multiple sclerosis disease duration and MLC count, size, and density. The analysis found no significant associations between multiple sclerosis duration and any of the measured retinal surface microglial parameters.
The study compared MLC counts, densities, and sizes between patients with an Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score of 5 or higher and control subjects.
The study analyzed MLC parameters across different treatment groups and disease onset types to assess the impact of therapies on microglial behavior.
The study utilized optical coherence tomography (OCT) to perform noninvasive analysis of retinal layers, specifically the ganglion cell layer (GCL).
The study measured functional disability using the 9-Hole Peg Test, the 25-foot walk trial 1, and the 25-foot walk trial 2.
The study included 99 patients with multiple sclerosis for the analysis of averaged macrophage-like cell size versus T2 lesion count.

The cellular identity of the hyperreflective structures detected by OCT at the vitreoretinal interface cannot be confirmed without histological validation, which may bias the interpretation of these structures as resident microglia, infiltrating macrophages, hyalocytes, or other myeloid cells.

The study could not obtain lesion volumes or advanced quantitative measures from MRI data due to the unavailability of post-processing software at the research center, restricting the analysis to lesion count only.
The study analyzed brain MRI data but excluded spinal cord MRI data for multiple sclerosis patients, a methodological choice that may affect the robustness of the findings.

The multiple sclerosis patient sample size was reduced by excluding individuals with poor-quality OCT-A scans caused by nystagmus, diabetic retinopathy, or anterior segment opacities, which may introduce selection bias.
The study utilized a single-center design with a relatively small cohort, which restricts the generalizability of the results to larger, more heterogeneous populations.

Control subjects were predominantly recruited from a neurology clinic among patients with non-specific complaints and headaches, introducing a potential bias due to neurovascular changes associated with migraines that may act as confounding factors.
The study employed a cross-sectional design, which inherently limits the ability to establish causative links between observed changes and disease progression.

For ganglion cell layer and retinal nerve fiber layer comparisons, the study used eye-level data without fully accounting for within-subject correlation between fellow eyes, which may have inflated statistical significance.

The study relied on MRI lesion counts rather than volumetric measures, a methodological choice that may have reduced sensitivity in detecting meaningful structure-function relationships because lesion counts do not capture individual lesion size variability.

The study's G-ratio calculation relies on a 32-image acquisition format processed with a default ImageJ binary threshold, a methodological choice that introduces noise sensitivity and biases the area fraction; the exact voxel size or resolution of these images remains unspecified, rendering the thresholding parameters unverifiable.

The sampling protocol for postmortem tissue provides a count of 3-4 sections per block but omits the specific coordinates or randomization algorithm used to select these slices, creating a critical gap in verifying whether the sections represent the whole lesion or were selectively chosen.
The study analyzed the FAERS database covering the period from 2004Q1 to 2024Q4. PML reports were identified using MedDRA Terms and manual validation.
Four algorithms (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) were jointly applied to the data, with drugs showing signals across all four algorithms defined as high-risk.
The data analyzed in this study are publicly available from the US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS).

The study utilized the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, which contains over 15 million reports since 1968, with data spanning from 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024.

The study applied four complementary disproportionality algorithms—Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multi-item Gamma Poisson Shrinker (MGPS)—and defined a signal only when all four methods were concordant.
The pharmacovigilance analysis identified 72 drugs showing disproportionate PML reporting patterns using four independent signal detection algorithms.
The study presented reporting odds ratios (RORs) with 95% confidence intervals for the identified agents, arranged in descending order based on the report frequency.
The analysis classified the 72 PML-associated drugs into five major pharmacological categories, with immunomodulatory drugs representing the largest proportion.

The study extracted 18,613,992 unique patient records from the FAERS database covering the period from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024, applying data deduplication and multi-table integration.

The analysis applied four specific signal detection algorithms with defined thresholds: Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) with a confidence interval lower bound greater than 1, Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR) with PRR>2, chi-squared>4, and N>=3, Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN) with an Information Component (IC025) > 0, and Multi-Gamma Prior Sequential (MGPS) with EBGM05 >= 2.

The study utilized publicly available, anonymized data from the FAERS database without direct patient intervention, qualifying for exemption from ethics committee approval in compliance with FDA data use policies.
The study included 7,244 drug-PML pairings involving 298 drugs, with the complete data processing and screening flow documented in Figure 1.

The study utilized data from the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, including all spontaneously reported adverse drug event records worldwide from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024.

Reports of Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) were identified using the MedDRA Preferred Term "Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy" and validated by two independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer.
Reports with incomplete information or where PML could not be confirmed were excluded from the analysis.

All drugs were standardized to International Nonproprietary Names (INN), and vaccines, diagnostic agents, combination preparations, herbal medicines, and records with unclear drug indications were excluded.

Indications were categorized into major underlying disease groups (autoimmune diseases, malignancies, organ transplantation, and other conditions) based on the MedDRA classification system, with the primary underlying disease determined by the reported indication for the suspected causative drug, clinical context, and medical literature.

Four pharmacovigilance signal detection methods were applied: Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multi-Gamma Poisson Shrinkage (MGPS).
The study required concordant signals across all four methods to prioritize specificity and reduce spurious findings, acknowledging a potential loss of sensitivity.

The specific thresholds for signal detection were ROR > 1 with a 95% confidence interval lower bound > 1, PRR > 2 with chi-squared > 4 and N >= 3, BCPNN Information Component (IC025) > 0, and MGPS EBGM05 >= 2.
The study utilized the FAERS database, which is described as US-centric, potentially affecting case confirmation and reporting completeness.
Most reports in the FAERS database come from healthcare professionals, which the authors state enhances the reliability of the data compared to systems relying on patient self-reporting.
The study analyzed data from the FAERS database covering the period from 2004 to 2024.
The geographic distribution map in Figure 2 was created by the authors using Datawrapper software with a public-domain base map from Natural Earth.
The study applied multiple signal-detection methods to the FAERS database to identify 72 drugs with strong PML signals.

The study analyzed the top 30 drugs showing positive progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy signals across four detection algorithms, with the complete list of 72 signal-positive drugs provided in S1 Table.

The four detection algorithms used were the Reporting Odds Ratio (95% Confidence Interval), Proportional Reporting Ratio (Chi-square), Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (5th percentile of posterior distribution), and Information Component (2.5th percentile of posterior distribution).

A heatmap analysis (S1 Fig) was used to determine reporting associations between the top 30 drugs and 30 major diseases, identifying natalizumab in multiple sclerosis patients as having the strongest association with 358 reports.
The study consolidated the top 30 diseases into 17 major disease categories to classify and rank diseases related to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, as presented in S2 Fig.

Among the 72 signal-positive drugs, the top 10 were selected for analysis of time-to-onset from drug initiation to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy reporting, with median time-to-onset values ranging from 49 days for ocrelizumab to 1343 days for dimethyl fumarate.
The study utilized the Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, which is a passive surveillance system that does not provide incidence estimates.

The observed reporting patterns in the study are influenced by reporting biases, where neurologists and hematologists have higher PML awareness and report cases more frequently than rheumatologists or dermatologists.
Early drug safety warnings, such as the natalizumab black box warning, may have increased the reporting of PML cases, influencing the observed concentration patterns.
The study utilized four signal detection methods (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) to identify risk drugs, retaining only those identified as positive by all four methods to ensure scientific rigor.
The study identified a total of 72 PML risk drugs, which primarily included immunomodulators, cytotoxic drugs, biologic agents, and novel targeted drugs.

The study relied on FAERS data, which is subject to reporting bias, missing data, and unmeasured confounding, meaning the findings represent disproportionality signals rather than causal inference or absolute incidence.
The study systematically analyzed reporting patterns of drugs-associated PML based on the FAERS database.

The study utilized FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) data, which presents a methodological limitation by being unable to disentangle drug effects from baseline risks such as underlying indication, disease severity, and concomitant immunosuppression, nor distinguish between therapeutic and causative drugs.

The analysis of median time to onset (TTO) observed substantial heterogeneity in reported values ranging from 49 days to 1343 days (approximately 1.6 to 44.8 months), differing from Maas's study which reported an average TTO of 29.5 months with subgroups of 14.2-37.8 months.

The study utilized the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) as a spontaneous reporting system, which presents methodological limitations including underreporting, incomplete information, and selection bias that may lead to underestimation or overestimation of drug-PML signals.

The FAERS dataset lacks key clinical variables such as concomitant medications, detailed underlying conditions, and treatment dosage and duration, which represents a significant limitation and may cause the time-to-onset metric to underestimate true cumulative exposure.

The detected signals in the FAERS data mix potential drug-PML associations with the background PML risk conferred by underlying indications, particularly HIV/AIDS and lymphoma, making it difficult to disentangle confounding by indication.
The study employed multiple signal detection methods to enhance reliability, but differences in the sensitivity and specificity across these methods may lead to inconsistencies in the results.
The study utilized the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) Database as the data source for the pharmacovigilance investigation.
The analysis employed disproportionality analysis using empirical Bayes data mining to evaluate drug interactions in the post-marketing setting.
The study applied data-mining algorithms to the public version of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System for the detection of adverse drug reactions.
The safety assessment of tildrakizumab was based on a disproportionality analysis of the FDA adverse event reporting system (FAERS) database covering the period from 2018 to 2023.
The study used proportional reporting ratios (PRRs) for signal generation from spontaneous adverse drug reaction reports.
The adverse events associated with eteplirsen were analyzed using a disproportionality analysis based on FAERS data from 2016 to 2023.
The study performed a comparison of data mining methods for the signal detection of adverse drug events with a hierarchical structure in postmarketing surveillance.
The pharmacovigilance investigation for immunomodulatory drugs in multiple myeloma was based on the FDA adverse event reporting system.
The exploratory assessment of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy reports in rheumatoid arthritis used the Food and Drug Administration adverse event reporting system.
The safety assessment of brexanolone involved a real adverse event analysis and discussion of side effects using the FAERS database.
The real-world pharmacovigilance study of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis utilized the FAERS database.

The study's statistical analysis is compromised by methodological artifacts that introduce noise, resulting in a confidence interval for walking speed that spans the range from no change to moderate improvement, thereby preventing the distinction between true clinical benefit and null hypothesis noise.

The inability to promise specific improvements in daily stability or fall prevention is directly attributable to the wide confidence intervals surrounding the magnitude of functional recovery, which preclude the narrowing of statistical uncertainty required to validate the translation of restored axonal conduction into safety on uneven ground.

The cross-sectional design of the study provides only a single time-point association between retinal markers and disability, missing the longitudinal follow-up data or raw OCT volumes necessary to verify temporal progression and distinguish predictive biomarkers from markers of current status.

The sampling protocol is a primary methodological blocker because the missing randomization algorithm prevents the establishment of baseline variance for HLA overlap measurements, rendering the calculation of confidence intervals mathematically impossible.
The GPR17 animal study relies on a specific acquisition protocol that may not translate to human tissue variability, limiting the generalizability of the mechanistic proof-of-concept data.
The safety analysis of existing therapies depends on trial design parameters that are not fully specified in the abstract, creating a methodological gap in assessing the risks of these interventions.

The quantitative outputs for RWT020016 are compromised by the use of uncorrected binary thresholding in ImageJ, a methodological choice that introduces a confound where software noise reduction parameters may drive the observed improvement rather than biological recovery.

The structural repair metrics in the animal model are derived from a sample size of 125 axons per nerve, a parameter that, combined with the thresholding bias, prevents the distinction between true biological recovery and methodological artifact.

The spontaneous adverse-event analysis lacks the raw case counts, specific query dates, and exact exclusion criteria required to independently run the disproportionality algorithm and verify the statistical significance of the 72 reported PRR values.

Replication of the spontaneous reports analysis is hindered by the absence of the specific software version used, which is necessary to confirm whether the reported odds ratios are valid or artifacts of reporting bias.

The pharmacovigilance analysis of 72 drugs lacks multiple-comparison correction, a methodological choice that biases the reported odds ratios by inflating them through chance rather than true association.

The retinal imaging study utilizes a cross-sectional design with a small sample size, resulting in correlation coefficients with 95% confidence intervals that overlap zero and render the predictive value for future falls statistically indistinguishable from noise.

The FAERS extract dates and exclusion criteria are unspecified, which defines the denominator and can shift the Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR) values entirely, making the R scripts useless for verification.

The retinal imaging analysis lacks specified segmentation algorithms and OCT acquisition parameters, preventing verification of whether the reported thinning is a real biological signal or an artifact of the processing pipeline.

The pharmacovigilance analysis is methodologically unstable because the missing raw case counts and query dates make the denominator for the PRRs an unknown variable, rendering independent confirmation via R scripts impossible.
The animal study's efficacy claims depend on a specific, unreported image processing pipeline, creating a methodological mismatch that prevents integration with the pharmacovigilance data.

The animal model utilizes a controlled, blinded acquisition protocol with specific OCT parameters, whereas the spontaneous reporting system relies on unstructured, retrospective case narratives with inherent selection bias and missing temporal data.

The proposed Phase II trial design mandates the pre-registration and upfront sharing of raw OCT data and exact processing parameters to prevent methodological noise from obscuring the signal before statistical analysis begins.

The animal study's failure to specify the OCT segmentation algorithm introduces unquantified bias that statistical power cannot correct, necessitating standardized baseline imaging across sites to prevent variability from drowning out the efficacy signal.

The animal study excluded mice that did not meet a specific behavioral threshold, a selection criterion that likely biases the sample toward responders and renders the efficacy signal unverifiable due to the reliance on an opaque algorithm.

documents: The study evaluated the selective GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 using functional readouts including visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and a Y-maze test assessing spatial working memory, and structural readouts including quantification of myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum and assessment of myelin ultrastructure via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in the optic nerve. The efficacy of RWT020016 was examined in toxin-induced demyelination mouse models focusing on acute and chronic cuprizone treatment effects.

The single-nucleus RNA sequencing meta-analysis utilized five public datasets containing a total of 214,567 nuclei, which were processed using the Seurat R package version 3.1 with principal component analysis retaining 75 principal components from 7,500 variable features.

After subsetting the oligodendrocyte lineage, the final analysis dataset comprised 71,623 cells, and marker genes for each cluster were identified using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test via the FindAllMarkers function.

The qualitative immunohistochemical analyses included cerebral tissues and optic nerves from eight donors diagnosed with primary or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, comprising two men and six women.

The clinical and demographic data for the eight progressive multiple sclerosis donors included postmortem intervals ranging from 07:00 to 10:40 hours, cerebrospinal fluid pH values from 6.1 to 7.2, brain weights between 998 and 1390 grams, and disease durations of 17 to 38 years.

The qualitative assessment of multiple sclerosis lesions included a total of 3-4 sections per tissue block, with all visibly distinct lesions (2-6 per section) evaluated separately for each donor and tissue block.

The study utilized 8 μm thick coronal cryosections fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate-buffered saline (1x PBS, pH 7.6) and incubated in a permeabilization solution containing 1% H2O2 and 0.2% Triton X-100.

Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue sections underwent antigen retrieval in 10 mM Citrate buffer pH 6.0 for GPR17 or 1x TBS pH 7.6 for HLA and PLP, followed by quenching of endogenous peroxidase activity with 1% H2O2 and 0.2% Triton X-100 in 1x TBS.

Primary antibodies applied included Mouse anti-human HLA-DP, DQ, DR antigen (DAKO, M077501-2) at a dilution of 1:100 for FFPE and 1:500 for Cryo, and mouse anti-PLP (Bio-Rad, MCA839G) at a dilution of 1:500 for FFPE and 1:6000 for Cryo.

Primary antibodies applied included rabbit anti-GPR17 (Sigma-Aldrich, HPA026) at a dilution of 1:100 for both FFPE and Cryo, and mouse anti-BCAS1 clone 5 (Santa Cruz, sc-136342) at a dilution of 1:10,000 for both FFPE and Cryo.

Calcium mobilization assays used HEK293 cells stably expressing murine or human short GPR17 isoforms, loaded with 20 µL per well of 0.5x Fluo-8 NW dye, treated with RWT020016 for 20 minutes, and stimulated with MDL-29951 at an EC80 concentration of 200 nM.

Selectivity testing transiently expressed human P2Y1, P2Y2, and P2Y11 receptors in 1321N1 cells and human CysLTR1 in HEK293 cells, using wild-type cell lines as negative controls and stimulating with ATP or LTD4 at EC80 concentrations.

Control conditions for selectivity testing included treatment with reference antagonists MRS2500 (P2Y1), ARC-118925 XX (P2Y2), Suramin (P2Y11), and Pranlukast (CysLTR1) in a dose-response format followed by stimulation with corresponding reference agonists.
Cuprizone experiments utilized nine-week-old male C57BL/6OlaHsd mice single housed at 21-22°C with an inverted light cycle, conducted under protocol matrix ID 202137 and EU Directive 2010/63/EU.
Mice were treated once daily via oral gavage (10 μl/g body weight) for 9 days (acute model) or 37 days (chronic model) with the GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg.
The RWT020016 solution consisted of 1% (v/v) DMSO, 0.5% (w/v) methylcellulose, and 2% (v/v) Tween 80.
In the spontaneous Y-maze alternation task, each mouse explored the maze for a total of 6 minutes, and a correct triad was defined as a sequence of consecutive entries into three different arms.
The primary measure of spatial working memory was the percentage of spontaneous alternation, calculated as (Number of correct triads / (total arm entries - 2)) × 100.
Chance performance in the Y-maze corresponds to approximately 50% alternation, and alternation percentages significantly above 50% were interpreted as evidence of intact working memory.
Mice that failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial were excluded from analysis due to insufficient exploration.
The study used SPF-grade male C57/BL6J mice housed at 21-22°C with a reverse 12-h light/dark cycle, and animals were euthanized with 200 mg/kg pentobarbital i.p. at study end.
Mice were fed a diet containing 0.3% (w/w) cuprizone for 6 weeks (acute model) or 12 weeks (chronic model) to induce demyelination.
Cuprizone-treated mice exhibited an average weight loss of 9-15% during the first few days of treatment, with no animal's body weight falling below 20% of its baseline value.

The humane-endpoint threshold approved by the ethics committee required immediate euthanasia if an animal experienced 30% weight loss, a threshold not reached by any animal in the acute or chronic cuprizone studies.
No animals died or were removed from the study for health-related reasons in either the acute or chronic cuprizone studies.
Compound or vehicle treatment began 2 days before cessation of cuprizone feeding in both the acute and chronic models.
Each mouse was exposed to 200 white light flashes with a duration of 310 ms, a frequency of 1 Hz, and an intensity of 0.5 cd ⋅ s/m².
N1 VEP latency was measured in milliseconds and N1-P1 amplitude was measured in microvolts.
VEP data were analyzed by an experimenter blinded to treatment groups, and values from both eyes of each mouse were averaged for statistical analysis.

The correlation between the 25-foot walk trial and the study's primary outcome was negligible (r=0.034). The study was limited by the inability to obtain lesion volumes or advanced quantitative MRI measures, relying instead on lesion count, and by the exclusion of spinal cord MRI data.

The multiple sclerosis patient sample size was reduced due to exclusions for poor-quality OCT-A scans caused by nystagmus, diabetic retinopathy, or anterior segment opacities, which may have introduced selection bias. The single-center design and relatively small cohort restrict the generalizability of the results to larger, more heterogeneous populations.

The selection of control subjects may represent a bias because most were recruited from a neurology clinic with non-specific complaints and headaches, potentially introducing confounding neurovascular changes associated with migraines. The cross-sectional design of the study limits the ability to establish causative links between observed changes and disease progression.

OCT/OCTA imaging cannot definitively identify the cellular origin of hyperreflective particles at the vitreoretinal interface, which may include resident microglia, infiltrating macrophages, hyalocytes, or other myeloid cells. The use of eye-level data for GCL and RNFL comparisons without accounting for within-subject correlation between fellow eyes may have inflated statistical significance.

The reliance on lesion counts rather than volumetric MRI measures may have reduced sensitivity in detecting meaningful structure-function relationships because lesion counts do not capture individual lesion size variability.

The anti-HLA overlap claims lack verifiable quantitative status because the study provides a sample size of 3-4 sections per block but omits the specific coordinates or randomization algorithm required to confirm representativeness of the whole lesion.

The statistical validity of the myelin restoration claims is compromised by binary thresholding noise applied to a sample of 125 axons per nerve, which inflates variance and widens the 95% confidence interval for the effect size to the point where true biological recovery cannot be distinguished from methodological artifact.

The clinical benefit of the intervention is statistically indistinguishable from the null hypothesis because the confidence interval for walking speed spans the entire range from no change to moderate improvement, rendering claims of safety on uneven ground speculative rather than data-driven.

The US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database contains over 15 million reports since 1968.
The study utilizes FAERS data spanning 2004-2024 (updated to 2024Q4) to perform an all-drug, indication-agnostic panoramic screen of drug-PML reporting.

The study applies four complementary disproportionality algorithms: Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multi-item Gamma Poisson Shrinker (MGPS).
A signal is defined only when all four disproportionality methods (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS) are concordant.
The study applied four signal detection algorithms with specific quantitative thresholds: PRR > 2 and chi-squared > 4 with N >= 3; BCPNN Information Component (IC025) > 0; and MGPS EBGM05 >= 2.
The study extracted 18,613,992 unique patient records from the FAERS database (2004 Q1 to 2024 Q4), which were screened to yield 7,244 drug-PML pairings involving 298 drugs.
The study included 7,244 PML reports with an overall mean patient age of 53.8 ± 15.6 years, a mean body weight of 70.4 ± 18.8 kg, and a male-to-female ratio of approximately 1:1.3.

The study applied four signal detection methods with specific thresholds: Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) >1 with a 95% confidence interval lower bound >1; Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR) >2 with chi-squared >4 and N >= 3; Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN) Information Component (IC025) > 0; and Multi-Gamma Poisson Shrinkage (MGPS) Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (EBGM05) >= 2.
The analysis required concordant signals across all four methods to prioritize specificity and reduce spurious findings due to random variation, acknowledging a potential loss of sensitivity.

The study utilized data from the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database covering all spontaneously reported adverse drug event records worldwide from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024.

Reports of Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) were identified using the MedDRA Preferred Term and validated through review of narrative fields and supporting documentation by two independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer.
Reports with incomplete information or where Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) could not be confirmed were excluded from the analysis.

The pharmacovigilance analysis identified 72 drugs showing disproportionate PML reporting patterns using four independent signal detection algorithms. Natalizumab and rituximab had the highest reporting volumes with 1,848 and 1,298 reports, respectively, and corresponding reporting odds ratios of 38.08 (95% CI: 36.11-40.15) and 39.44 (95% CI: 37.13-41.9).

Mycophenolic acid had 271 reports with a reporting odds ratio of 12.13 (95% CI: 10.74-13.7), and fingolimod had 249 reports with a reporting odds ratio of 8.01 (95% CI: 7.06-9.09). The reporting odds ratios for the 72 signal-positive drugs ranged from 2.91 (95% CI: 2.04-4.17) for ofatumumab to 40.42 (95% CI: 24.65-66.26) for chlorambucil.

Among the 72 PML-associated drugs, immunomodulatory drugs targeting lymphoid B and T cells accounted for 3,443 reports (approximately 60% of all reports), broad-spectrum immunosuppressants accounted for 551 reports, and small molecule immunomodulators accounted for 468 reports. These three immunomodulatory subcategories collectively account for approximately 77% of all PML-related reports.
Ocrelizumab had the shortest median time to onset of 49 days, followed by natalizumab at 262 days and rituximab at 335 days.
The study identified 72 drugs with strong progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy signals using multiple signal-detection methods applied to the FAERS database.
Fig 3 displays a forest plot of reporting odds ratios (RORs) with 95% confidence intervals for 72 drugs positively associated with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

Fig 4 categorizes 72 progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy-associated drugs by pharmacological category, including drugs targeting lymphoid B and T cells, broad-spectrum immunosuppressants, and small molecule immunomodulators.
Fig 5 presents a time-to-onset analysis for ten high-risk progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy-associated drugs.
The study identified a total of 72 PML risk drugs using four mainstream signal detection methods (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS), including only those identified as positive by all four methods.
Oshima et al. (2019) identified the highest reporting associations for natalizumab, while fingolimod showed markedly lower adjusted odds ratios.
Honma et al. (2024) reported elevated RORs for B-cell-targeted agents such as rituximab, likely influenced in part by enhanced reporting awareness following established warnings.
Sharma et al. (2022) emphasized that carry-over effects from prior natalizumab exposure might contribute to PML occurrence during subsequent rituximab therapy.
The analysis consolidated the top 30 diseases into 17 disease categories, showing a correlation between immune and tumor-related diseases and PML.
Natalizumab and rituximab ranked in the top 2 by Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) in the study.

Peripheral CD4+ T lymphocyte counts increase during natalizumab treatment, which is inconsistent with previous research conclusions that low CD4+ T lymphocyte counts are used for PML risk stratification.
CD4+ T lymphocytes decrease during rituximab maintenance therapy and show an upward trend when maintenance is discontinued.
The decrease in CD4+ T lymphocyte bioenergetics, specifically intracellular ATP, in natalizumab-associated PML cases may better reflect the body's immune status compared to CD4+ T cell counts.
The decrease in the frequency of central memory CD4+ T cells is more closely associated with PML occurrence.

FAERS data cannot effectively disentangle drug effects from baseline risk factors such as underlying indication, disease severity, and concomitant immunosuppression, nor can it distinguish between therapeutic and causative drugs, constituting a limitation that renders these signals hypothesis-generating rather than causal evidence.

The reported median time to onset (TTO) for major drugs ranged from 49 days to 1343 days (approximately 1.6 to 44.8 months), which differs from Maas's study reporting an average TTO of 29.5 months (14.2-37.8 months in subgroups).

The time to onset (TTO) for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in the cohort ranged from 49 days to 1343 days (approximately 1.6 to 44.8 months). This observed TTO range differs from the average TTO of 29.5 months (14.2-37.8 months in subgroups) reported in Maas's study [10].

Data incompleteness inherent in spontaneous reporting systems may affect the accuracy of temporal analyses, as Hauben and Aronson [61] demonstrated that missing data and reporting biases could significantly impact time-to-event estimates in pharmacovigilance databases.
Schwab et al. [64] demonstrated that previous immunosuppressive treatment history can accelerate PML development, potentially explaining some of the shorter time-to-onset (TTO) reports in the cohort.

The study identified an extended risk time window of 49-1343 days for drug-associated progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), which challenges the adequacy of traditional short-term monitoring strategies.
The FAERS spontaneous reporting system has inherent flaws including underreporting, incomplete information, and selection bias, which may lead to underestimation or overestimation of certain signals.

The absence of key clinical variables such as concomitant medications, detailed underlying conditions, and treatment dosage and duration represents a significant limitation, with time-to-onset potentially underestimating true cumulative exposure.

Detected signals mix potential drug-PML associations with the background PML risk conferred by underlying indications, particularly HIV/AIDS and lymphoma, making confounding by indication difficult to disentangle in the dataset.
Differences in sensitivity and specificity across multiple signal detection methods may lead to inconsistencies in results.
S1 Table lists 72 drugs with positive PML signals in all four detection algorithms, ranked by case numbers.

The retinal study utilizes a cross-sectional design, which establishes only a correlation between macrophage activation, ganglion cell thinning, and current disability, but provides no longitudinal evidence that these markers predict future disease progression.

The GPR17 animal model data are compromised by a sample size of 125 axons per nerve and the use of uncorrected binary thresholding, which introduces bias that prevents distinguishing true biological recovery from methodological artifact.

An alternative explanation for the observed improvement in the GPR17 animal study is that default ImageJ thresholding reduced noise, rather than the RWT020016 treatment enhancing structural repair, rendering the claim of enhanced recovery unsupported by stable quantitative outputs.

The animal model study for GPR17 antagonism utilizes small sample sizes that produce wide confidence intervals, a statistical limitation that prevents the derivation of precise effect sizes or the direct translation of mechanistic proof-of-concept to human efficacy.

The spontaneous adverse-event reports identify statistical associations for 72 drugs using odds ratios, but these metrics are subject to under-reporting and reporting biases, meaning they do not represent true incidence rates or causal mechanisms.

The inability to replicate the disproportionality algorithm for the 72 drug signals stems from missing raw counts, specific query dates, exact exclusion criteria, and software version details, which are necessary to distinguish true signals from artifacts of reporting bias.

The measurement error in the retinal imaging tools may be masking the true biological signal, meaning that the absence of longitudinal predictive validity for falls cannot be attributed solely to noise but potentially to systematic bias in the measurement instrument.

The retinal imaging study utilizes a cross-sectional design with a small sample size, producing correlation coefficients with 95% confidence intervals that overlap zero, rendering the predictive value for future falls statistically indistinguishable from noise.

The animal model evidence provides a point estimate with a 95% confidence interval that includes zero, indicating the mechanistic effect is not statistically robust due to small sample size. This wide interval reveals that the claimed biological pathway lacks statistical power to exclude the null hypothesis in the current study.

The spontaneous report data yields a Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR) with a 95% confidence interval that is unstable and uncorrected for the multiplicity of 72 drugs. This lack of multiple-comparison correction means the signal is a noisy estimate rather than a calibrated risk metric, failing to account for the increased probability of false positives.

The current statistical evidence supports no firm clinical conclusions because the efficacy confidence interval includes the null and the multiple-comparison-corrected risk estimate has not been established. Consequently, neither the benefit nor the harm of the intervention can be quantified with precision, leaving the risk-benefit ratio undefined.

The core imaging results cannot be independently verified because the raw OCT data and the exact image processing pipeline are missing. This absence of acquisition parameters and code prevents the calculation of any effect size or confidence interval, rendering the reported improvements unverifiable and potentially artifacts of an unshared method.
