documents: The funder provided financial support in the form of salaries for authors DDH, EL, VB, RP, and GD, but did not have any additional role in the study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.
The synthetic small molecule ligand MDL-29951 was included in the study, revealing a competitive antagonism of RWT020016.
The study utilized the small molecule GPR17 antagonist RWT020016, which was included in the study to reveal competitive antagonism of MDL-29951.
Previous non-selective GPR17 antagonists used in early studies included Pranlukast and Montelukast.
Histamine H3 antagonists Clemastine and GSK239512 were associated with off-target side effects of fatigue and insomnia in past clinical trials.
The antibody Elezanumab targeting RGMa was limited by insufficient brain exposure, and Bexarotene was associated with metabolic disturbances in past trials.
The study evaluated the GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 in toxin-induced demyelination mouse models using acute and chronic cuprizone treatment.
Functional readouts for the RWT020016 study included visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and a Y-maze test assessing spatial working memory.

Structural readouts for the RWT020016 study included quantification of myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum and assessment of myelin ultrastructure via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in the optic nerve.
GPR17 expression was characterized in postmortem human brain and optic nerve tissue using single-nucleus RNA sequencing data.
Five public single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets were used to generate a total of 214,567 nuclei, with raw count matrices obtained from their respective repositories.
Data preprocessing and integration were performed using the Seurat R package version 3.1, applying standard quality control metrics to exclude low-quality nuclei.
Dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis (PCA) with 7,500 variable features and 75 principal components retained for downstream analysis.
Cells were embedded using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) based on the integrated PCA space, and clustering was performed using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions.
The final dataset contained 71,623 cells after subsetting the oligodendrocyte lineage and repeating integration, dimensionality reduction, and clustering steps.

Marker genes for each cluster were identified using Seurat's FindAllMarkers function with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and differential expression analyses between selected clusters were performed using FindMarkers with the same statistical framework.

Human brain tissues for the immunohistochemical analysis were provided by the Netherlands Brain Bank (NBB, Amsterdam, The Netherlands) and accessed between 01.01.1996 and 31.12.2018. The use of these autoptic samples was approved by the Ethics Committee of Amsterdam UMC (IRB number: IRB00002991; Federal-wide Assurance number: 00003703).

The qualitative immunohistochemical analyses included cerebral tissues and optic nerves from eight donors diagnosed with primary or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS or SPMS), consisting of two men and six women. Clinical and demographic characteristics for these donors are summarized in Table 1.

Double immunostaining was performed on sections from all dissected tissue blocks to visualize proteolipid protein (PLP) and human leukocyte antigen (HLA-DR-DQ, referred to as HLA) for the classification of demyelinating lesions.

Table 1 lists specific clinical and demographic data for the eight progressive multiple sclerosis donors, including donor ID, clinical diagnosis, age, sex, post-mortem delay (PMD) in hours, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pH, brain weight in grams, disease duration in years, cause of death, specific tissue type, and fixation method (FFPE or Cryo).

White matter and cortical grey matter multiple sclerosis lesions were characterized according to the system established by Kuhlmann et al. [52], with innate inflammatory lesion activity determined by the presence of HLA+ microglia/macrophages as described by the Neuroimmunology Research Group at the Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience [50,51].

Cryosectioning involved cutting coronal sections 8 µm thick, fixing them in 4% paraformaldehyde in 1x phosphate-buffered saline (pH 7.6), and incubating them in a permeabilization solution of 1% H2O2 and 0.2% Triton X-100 in 1x PBS.

Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections were deparaffinized and processed for antigen retrieval in 10 mM Citrate buffer pH 6.0 for GPR17 or 1x TBS pH 7.6 for HLA and PLP, followed by quenching endogenous peroxidase with 1% H2O2 and 0.2% Triton X-100 in 1x TBS.

The primary antibodies used were Mouse anti-human HLA-DP, DQ, DR antigen (DAKO, M077501-2; FFPE dilution 1:100, Cryo dilution 1:500), mouse anti-PLP (Bio-Rad, MCA839G; FFPE dilution 1:500, Cryo dilution 1:6000), rabbit anti-GPR17 (Sigma-Aldrich, HPA026; FFPE and Cryo dilution 1:100), and mouse anti-BCAS1 clone 5 (Santa Cruz, sc-136342; FFPE and Cryo dilution 1:10,000).
The chemical structure of the test compound RWT020016 cannot be disclosed by Rewind Therapeutics NV due to strategic and legal constraints, which blocks replication of the compound synthesis.
Single-dose pharmacokinetic studies for RWT020016 were performed by CRO Pharmaron Inc. using standard industry NeuroPK protocols with N=3 subjects and a dose volume of 5 ml/kg.

Plasma samples for RWT020016 pharmacokinetic analysis were obtained by terminal cardiac puncture, while brain tissues were collected following exsanguination and saline perfusion to minimize residual blood contamination.
Plasma and brain homogenate concentrations of RWT020016 were quantified using a validated LC-MS/MS method.

Pharmacokinetic parameters for RWT020016, including bioavailability, maximum concentration, time to maximum concentration, terminal half-life, area under the concentration-time curve, and brain-to-plasma ratios, were calculated using noncompartmental analysis.
cAMP accumulation assays for RWT020016 were performed by CRO Eurofins DiscoverX using CHO-K1 cells stably expressing the recombinant murine GPR17 receptor.
Dose-response curves for RWT020016 were generated at eight concentrations, each tested in duplicate, in the cAMP HTRF potency assay.

For antagonist testing of RWT020016, cells were preincubated with RWT020016 for 10 min, followed by the addition of a mixture containing forskolin (1 μM) and the GPR17 agonist MDL-29951 (EC80, 200 nM).
After 30 min incubation at room temperature, lysis buffer containing cAMP-d2 and anti-cAMP cryptate detection reagent (Cisbio #62AM4PEJ) was added to the RWT020016 assay plates.

The RWT020016 assay plates were incubated for 1 h at room temperature, and fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) ratios were measured using the HTRF kit according to the manufacturer's protocol.

The test compound RWT020016 was synthesized by CRO Pharmaron Inc. via standard solution-phase synthesis from commercially available building blocks, followed by chromatographic purification and routine analytical characterization. The chemical structure of RWT020016 cannot be disclosed by Rewind Therapeutics NV due to strategic and legal constraints, which blocks replication.

Full synthetic procedures for the GPR17 antagonists are described in patents WO2022254027 and WO2024115733. The compounds were obtained as pharmaceutically relevant forms, including salts, solvates, and polymorphs, designed to balance lipophilicity and polarity for CNS exposure.

Brightfield images of 3,3-diaminobenzidine (DAB)-stained sections were acquired using an Axio Scan Z.1 microscope (Zeiss) equipped with Neoplanfluor objectives and recorded with an Evolution MP camera (Media Cybernetics). Fluorescent images were obtained using an Axio Scan Z.1 (Zeiss) with a Plan-Apochromat 20x/0.8 M27 objective and an Evolution black-and-white camera (MediaCybernetics), with analysis performed using ImagePro software.
For qualitative assessment, 3-4 sections per tissue block (neocortex and optic nerves) were included, and all visibly distinct lesions (2-6 per section) were evaluated separately.

Immunostaining protocols used anti-PLP (Bio-Rad, MCA839G) at 1:500 for FFPE and 1:6000 for Cryo sections, rabbit anti-GPR17 (Sigma-Aldrich, HPA026) at 1:100 for both FFPE and Cryo, and mouse anti-BCAS1 clone 5 (Santa Cruz, sc-136342) at 1:10,000 for both FFPE and Cryo. Secondary antibodies included biotinylated horse anti-mouse or anti-rabbit (Vector Laboratories) at 1:400, HRP-mouse EnVision kit (DAKO, K5007), DAB EnVision kit at 1:50, Donkey anti-mouse IgG Cy3 at 1:600, and donkey anti-rabbit IgG DyLight 649 at 1:800.

Sections for double immunofluorescence stainings were incubated in Hoechst at 1:1000 in 1x PBS pH 7.6, followed by 0.1% Sudan Black, and mounted in Mowiol (EMD Chemicals). DAB-stained sections were dehydrated through an ethanol and xylene series and mounted with Entellan (Sigma-Aldrich).

Calcium mobilization assays were performed by Axxam S.p.A. using a Molecular Devices FLIPR TETRA ICCD camera, with automated liquid handling via Hamilton Microlab STAR, CyBio Felix, and CyBio Well Vario systems.
HEK293 cells stably expressing murine or human short GPR17 isoforms were loaded with 20 µL per well of 0.5x Fluo-8 NW dye (AAT Bioquest) in Tyrode's buffer and incubated for 1 hour at 37 °C.
Cells were treated with RWT020016 in a dose-response format for 20 minutes, followed by stimulation with the GPR17 agonist MDL-29951 at its EC80 concentration of 200 nM.

For selectivity testing, human P2Y1, P2Y2, and P2Y11 receptors were transiently expressed in 1321N1 cells, and human CysLTR1 was transiently expressed in HEK293 cells, with corresponding wild-type cell lines serving as negative controls.

Selectivity assays involved treating cells with RWT020016 in a dose-response format for 20 minutes, followed by stimulation with ATP for P2Y receptors or LTD4 for CysLTR1 at their respective EC80 concentrations.

Control conditions included treatment with reference antagonists MRS2500 for P2Y1, ARC-118925 XX for P2Y2, Suramin for P2Y11, and Pranlukast for CysLTR1 in a dose-response format before stimulation with corresponding reference agonists.
Fluorescence signals were recorded in real time and analyzed using Genedata Screener software (Genedata AG), with results expressed as a percentage effect relative to normalization standards.
Cuprizone experiments were conducted at the Hasselt University animal facility under protocols approved by the local Ethical Committee (matrix ID: 202137) and EU Directive 2010/63/EU.

Nine-week-old male C57BL/6OlaHsd mice (Envigo/Inotiv) were single housed under standard enriched conditions with ad libitum access to food and water, at a controlled temperature of 21-22°C and an inverted light cycle.

NeuroPK experiments utilized SPF-grade male C57/BL6J mice (Zhejiang Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd, license number: SCXK (浙) 2020-0002) maintained under a reverse 12-h light/dark cycle at 21-22°C with ad libitum food and water access.
Animals were euthanized at study end using pentobarbital at a dose of 200 mg/kg administered intraperitoneally.

Cuprizone-induced demyelination was achieved by feeding mice a pelleted diet containing 0.3% (w/w) cuprizone (Bis(cyclohexanone)oxaldihydrazone; Sigma-Aldrich, C9012-25G) formulated by Bio-Services/Sniff for either 6 weeks (acute model) or 12 weeks (chronic model).
Control animals received an identical standard diet without cuprizone, and compound or vehicle treatment began 2 days before cessation of cuprizone feeding in both models.

The selective GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 was dissolved in a vehicle consisting of 1% (v/v) DMSO, 0.5% (w/v) methylcellulose (M0512, Sigma-Aldrich), and 2% (v/v) Tween 80 (P1754, Sigma-Aldrich), and delivered at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg via oral gavage (10 µl/g body weight) for 9 days in the acute model or 37 days in the chronic model.

Spatial working memory was assessed using the spontaneous Y-maze alternation task at the end of the demyelination (week 6 and week 12) and remyelination (week 7 and week 17) periods in the acute and chronic cuprizone models, respectively, following the protocol published in reference [57].

In the Y-maze task, each mouse was placed in an arm facing the center and allowed to explore for 6 minutes, with an arm entry recorded when both hind paws fully entered an arm and a correct triad defined as a sequence of consecutive entries into three different arms.
The primary measure of spatial working memory was the percentage of spontaneous alternation, calculated using the formula: (Number of correct triads / (total arm entries - 2)) * 100.
Mice that failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial were excluded from analysis due to insufficient exploration.

The statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism for Windows version 10.2.1, with data presented as mean values plus or minus the standard error of the mean (SEM) and a significance threshold of p < 0.05.
The reference value for normal mitochondrial density was established at an average of 0.15 per µm², which is equivalent to 30 mitochondria per 200 µm².

The cumulative pathology score for optic nerve images was classified into grade 1 (score 2-3), grade 2 (score 3-4), grade 3 (score 4-5), and grade 4 (score 5-6) based on the average score per optic nerve.

Mouse optic nerves were fixed at week 17 of the chronic cuprizone study using a lethal injection of 200 mg/kg pentobarbital (i.p.) and cardiac perfusion. The optic nerves were immersed overnight at 4°C in 2% glutaraldehyde in 0.05 M sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 7.3), washed in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer, and post-fixed in 2% osmium tetroxide in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer for 60 minutes.

After dehydration through ascending concentrations of ethanol, optic nerves were incubated in propylene oxide for 60 minutes, infiltrated overnight with a 1:1 mixture of propylene oxide and epoxy resin, embedded in Epon, and polymerized at 60°C for 48 hours. Ultrathin cross-sections (60-80 nm) were cut on a Reichert Ultracut microtome, mounted on copper grids, and stained with lead citrate.

For each optic nerve, five images of optic nerve sections per mouse were randomly selected and analyzed in a blinded manner using Fiji ImageJ software. The g-ratio was calculated as the ratio of the inner axonal diameter ($d_{axon}$) to the total outer diameter of the myelinated fiber including the myelin sheath ($d_{fiber}$).

G-ratios were measured for 25 axons per image to assess myelin thickness using Fiji (ImageJ). Ultrastructural pathology was assessed using a semi-quantitative TEM-based scoring system detailed in Table 2.

In a previous pilot study, the numerical density of axons containing mitochondria was assessed within 5 images of 200 μm² size per animal (n=5), yielding an average of 0.15/μm² (equivalent to 30 per 200 μm²). This value was used as the reference for normal mitochondrial density and morphology in the current study.

The study utilizes a standard MS lesion scoring system with codes 0-6 to classify lesions, such as code 3 for mixed active/inactive lesions and code 5II for cortical grey matter lesions. The figures are available at https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0354525.g001 and https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0354525.g002.

GPR17 expression was not quantified across lesion types because limited sample numbers and inter-patient heterogeneity prevented statistically robust or biologically meaningful quantitative comparisons.
The single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis combined data from five human brain studies, including a total of 214,567 cells with a specific population of 71,623 oligodendrocyte lineage cells.

Cluster identities in the single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis were validated using specific marker genes: FYB1 and C3 for microglia, AQP4 and GJA1 for astrocytes, MOBP and MBP for oligodendrocytes, GRIN1, GAD2, and SLC17A7 for neurons, and CLDN5 for endothelial cells.

Lineage progression from oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) to non-fibrillar oligodendrocytes (NFOLs) was confirmed by the expression of stage-specific markers SOX6, BMP4, TNS3, TCF7L2, CASR, FYN, and ITPR2.

Committed oligodendrocyte precursors (COPs) were characterized by higher GPR17 expression compared to OPCs, alongside the presence of markers associated with early differentiation stages, including FYN kinase and myelin-related genes PLP1 and MBP.

Brain and optic nerve sections were stained for GPR17, HLA/PLP, and BCAS1 (Brain Enriched Myelin Associated Protein 1) to investigate the spatial relationship between GPR17 expression and multiple sclerosis lesion pathology.
Lesions in the brain tissue were classified according to established histopathological criteria published by Luchetti et al. [51] based on demyelination status and microglia/macrophage activity.

Figure 1B presents a UMAP plot of single nucleus RNA sequencing data from the combined dataset of five human brain studies, showing GPR17 expression per cell as a color gradient along UMAP1 and UMAP2 axes.
Mice were excluded from analysis if they failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial in the ic cuprizone model.

Anesthesia for visual evoked potential (VEP) recordings was induced via intraperitoneal injection of 5 µl/g body weight of xylazine (10 mg/kg, Rompun) and ketamine (70 mg/kg, Anesketin, Eurovet) dissolved in saline.
Pupillary dilation for VEP recordings was achieved using 0.5% tropicamide (Monofree Tropimide, Thea Pharma) followed by 10% phenylephrine (Thea Pharma).

For VEP electrophysiological setup, a subdermal recording electrode was inserted over the visual cortex, a reference electrode was placed in the tongue, and a ground electrode was placed at the base of the tail.
Each mouse was exposed to 200 white light flashes with a duration of 310 ms, a frequency of 1 Hz, and an intensity of 0.5 cd ⋅ s/m² during VEP recordings.
VEP recordings were performed in complete darkness inside a Faraday cage using the CELERIS system (Diagnosys), and data were analyzed using Diagnosys ESPION software (Diagnosys).
VEP traces were analyzed offline by identifying the N1 peak latency and measuring the N1-P1 peak-to-peak amplitude, with values from both eyes of each mouse averaged for statistical analysis.
Mice were perfused intracardially with saline after a 200 mg/kg intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital, and brains were post-fixed overnight in 4% PFA.

Brain sections were prepared by incubating in a graded sucrose series (10%, 20% and 30%), embedding in optimal cutting temperature medium (Tissue Tec, VWR), and cutting coronal cryosections at 5 µm thickness at Bregma -2.0 mm.
Cryosections were fixed in ice-cold acetone and incubated with blocking buffer consisting of 0.05% Triton X-100 (Thermofisher Scientific) and 10% DAKO protein block in PBS (DAKO).

Overnight incubation was performed with primary antibodies rat anti-myelin basic protein (MBP; MAB386, Millipore, 1:500) or rabbit anti-GPR17 (10136, Sanbio Cayman Chemicals, 1:200), both diluted in blocking buffer.
Secondary antibodies used were anti-rat Alexa 555 (A21434, Life Technologies, 1:400) for MBP or anti-rabbit Alexa 555 (A31572, Life Technologies, 1:400) for GPR17, both diluted in 1x PBS.
Slides were counterstained with DAPI and mounted using Fluoromount G (00-4958-02, Life Technologies), and images were acquired with a Leica DM2000 LED fluorescence microscope.

Quantification of MBP and GPR17 immunoreactivity used a 32-image format in ImageJ (Fiji) with the default thresholding plugin to measure the area fraction above threshold within a fixed-dimension square in the medial corpus callosum at Bregma -2.0 mm.

The cuprizone model used 0.3% concentration for 6 weeks (acute) or 12 weeks (chronic), followed by 1 week or 5 weeks of spontaneous remyelination on normal placebo pellets, with compound treatment initiated two days prior to cuprizone withdrawal.

Visual evoked potential (VEP) latency and amplitude were assessed at baseline, at the end of the demyelination phase (week 6 for acute, week 12 for chronic), and at the end of the remyelination phase (week 7 for acute, week 17 for chronic).
Mice were subjected to the Y-maze spontaneous alternation test at the end of the demyelination phase to evaluate cognitive processing speed and episodic memory deficits.
Myelin basic protein (MBP) immunohistochemical expression was evaluated in the medial corpus callosum to investigate structural changes in myelin following acute and chronic cuprizone exposure.
RWT020016 was evaluated for selectivity against hCYSLTR1, P2Y1, P2Y2, and P2Y11 receptors using the CEREP SafetyScreen87 panel from Eurofins, which contains 87 molecular targets.

In the CEREP SafetyScreen87 panel, RWT020016 was tested at a concentration of 10 µM, and follow-up functional studies at Eurofins identified an IC50 of 4 µM for 5-HT2A antagonism and an EC50 of 9.9 µM for KOR agonism.
Pharmacokinetic studies of RWT020016 in C57BL/6 mice involved a single oral administration at a dose of 3 mg/kg.
RWT020016 demonstrated a bioavailability of 91%, peak plasma concentrations exceeding 12,000 ng/mL, and an unbound brain-to-plasma ratio greater than 0.05 in C57BL/6 mice.
RWT020016 is an undisclosed small molecule GPR17 antagonist selected from the lead optimization of a sulfonamide series published by Rewind Therapeutics (references 53, 54).

The potency of RWT020016 was evaluated using cAMP accumulation assays with the synthetic agonist MDL-29951, yielding an IC50 of 21 nM for human short isoform GPR17 (s-GPR17), 34 nM for human long isoform GPR17 (l-GPR17), and 225 nM for murine GPR17.
In calcium mobilization assays, RWT020016 demonstrated IC50 values of 60 nM for s-GPR17 Gai signaling, 75 nM for Gaq signaling, and 142 nM for murine GPR17.
RWT020016 showed weak activity on mock-transfected cells in calcium mobilization assays, confirming that the observed activity is specific to GPR17.

The pharmacokinetic profile of RWT020016 was measured at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg, with brain exposure time points at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours following single oral administration in mice, using N=3 per time point.

The acute cuprizone model involved 6 weeks of cuprizone treatment followed by 1 week of RWT020016 or vehicle administration, while the chronic model involved 12 weeks of cuprizone treatment followed by 35 days of daily oral dosing of RWT020016 or vehicle.
Visual evoked potential (VEP) latency was the primary functional outcome measure, with the acute model assessing recovery at week 7 and the chronic model assessing recovery at week 17.
Spatial working memory was assessed using a spontaneous alternation task, with the acute model evaluated at week 7 and the chronic model evaluated at week 17.
The criteria for brain penetration in non-perfused brain tissue require an unbound brain-to-plasma ratio exceeding 0.05 and an effect(C_max) exceeding 12,000 ng/mL.

In the in vivo cuprizone experiments, the average total level of RWT020016 measured in the brain 2 hours after dosing was 56.6 ng/g (SD=15.8) for the 0.3 mg/kg dose and 232.2 ng/g (SD=89.5) for the 1 mg/kg dose.
The acute cuprizone model involves 6 weeks of cuprizone treatment, and the chronic cuprizone model involves 12 weeks of demyelination.
Quantification of relative GPR17 protein expression in the corpus callosum used an unpaired t-test with N=9-11 for the acute model and N=9-11 for the chronic model.
Data for relative GPR17 protein expression are presented as mean ± SEM and as fold-change relative to the control mean, with the mean control values set to 1.0.

RWT020016 exhibits an IC50 of 60 nM for human short-GPR17 with Gi coupling and 75 nM for human short-GPR17 with Gq coupling in calcium mobilization assays. The compound shows an IC50 of 142 nM for mouse GPR17 with Gq coupling in calcium mobilization assays.
In cAMP assays, RWT020016 has an IC50 of 21 nM for human short-GPR17, 34 nM for human long-GPR17, and 225 nM for mouse GPR17.

RWT020016 demonstrates selectivity against closely related Class A GPCRs with IC50 values greater than 49.8 μM for antagonism and agonism of human cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 (hCYSLTR1), human purinergic receptor P2Y1 (hP2RY1), human purinergic receptor P2Y2 (hP2RY2), and human purinergic receptor P2Y11 (hP2RY11).

RWT020016 has a molecular weight of less than 500 g/mol, 2 hydrogen bond donors, fewer than 10 hydrogen bond acceptors, and a cLogP of less than 5. After single-dose oral administration at 0.3 mg/kg, RWT020016 has a half-life of 8.3 hours, a brain Tmax of 1 hour, a brain Cmax of 39 ng/g, and a brain AUC0-24h of 588 h·ng/g.
After single-dose oral administration at 1 mg/kg, RWT020016 has a half-life of 6.9 hours, a brain Tmax of 2 hours, a brain Cmax of 205 ng/g, and a brain AUC0-24h of 2408 h·ng/g.

RWT020016 was administered at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg to mice in acute and chronic cuprizone demyelination models, with statistical comparisons performed using One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test or one-sample t-tests against a 50% chance level.
The study utilized sample sizes of N=10-11 for visual evoked potential (VEP) latency measurements and N=9-11 for working memory assessments in the acute and chronic cuprizone models.
RWT020016 was administered at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg to evaluate its effect on myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum.
MBP expression was assessed by immunofluorescence staining at week 7 for the acute cuprizone model and week 17 for the chronic cuprizone model.
The quantitative analysis of MBP protein expression used a One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test with sample sizes of N=10-11.
Data for MBP protein expression are presented as mean ± SEM relative to the control mean, with control values set to 100%.
RWT020016 treatment at a dose of 1 mg/kg significantly decreased the G-ratio in the optic nerve at week 17 of the chronic cuprizone model (p=0.049 vs. vehicle).
The study utilized a semi-quantitative transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis to assess structural changes in the optic nerve, specifically focusing on the chronic cuprizone model.

The vehicle-treated group exhibited a substantial increase in the proportion of optic nerves displaying moderate to severe pathology (Grades 3-4), characterized by mitochondria with altered morphology, loose or disintegrating myelin, and degenerating axons.

RWT020016 treatment at 1 mg/kg markedly reduced the proportion of optic nerves with high-grade pathology and specifically reduced the number of axons with loose or detached myelin sheaths relative to the vehicle group.
RWT020016 is described as an orally active, potent, selective, and specific GPR17 antagonist that achieves effective target blockade at a dose of 1 mg/kg.
RWT0202016 was administered at a dose of 1 mg/kg in cuprizone demyelination mouse models.
The study used a cuprizone demyelination model that does not recapitulate the full inflammatory complexity of demyelinating diseases, which is a gap for replication in broader contexts.
Transmission electron microscopy analysis of the optic nerve involved quantifying G-ratios of 125 axons per optic nerve from five TEM images per optic nerve section.
The semi-quantitative analysis of optic nerve pathology used a scoring system for grades 1 (none), 2 (mild), 3 (moderate), and 4 (severe) with sample sizes of N=6-7.
Statistical analysis of G-ratios used a One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test with N=6.
The study used 5 publicly available single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets derived from postmortem human brain to confirm GPR17's selective expression in oligodendrocyte lineage cells.
The screening assays used cAMP and Ca2+ levels as readouts for downstream signaling events mediated by Gai/o and Gaq proteins to measure the potency of RWT020016.
The study utilized a cuprizone diet to induce demyelination and assessed functional recovery using VEP recordings and spatial working memory behavioral tests.

Reproduction of the single-nucleus RNA sequencing analysis requires the specific marker genes listed in Figure S1, including FYB1, C3, AQP4, GJA1, MOBP, MBP, GRIN1, GAD2, SLC17A7, CLDN5, SOX6, BMP4, TNS3, and FYN.
The single-nucleus RNA sequencing data in Figure S1 uses log-normalized counts for gene expression levels, visualized via UMAP plots for glial cells from five different integrated datasets.
The study utilized VEP, behavioural assessment, histology, and ultrastructural analysis of myelin repair to evaluate the effects of RWT020016.

The study utilized male mice only to reduce biological variability, which limits the generalizability of the findings and requires future studies to include both sexes to assess sex-dependent differences in pharmacokinetics, target engagement, and remyelination efficacy.
Replication of the myelin basic protein data requires additional ultrastructural investigations in the corpus callosum, which is a white matter structure strongly affected by the cuprizone treatment.

Confirming that GPR17 antagonism promotes the differentiation of COPs to myelinating oligodendroglia requires immunohistochemical and volumetric cellular density analyses using markers of mature oligodendrocytes.

Quantifying GPR17+ cell density is not an optimal measure for drug target engagement because GPR17 expression does not undergo autoregulatory feedback in response to pharmacological inhibition and exposure to a GPR17 antagonist does not alter the number of GPR17+ oligodendroglial cells.
Direct assessment of downstream signaling events in GPR17-expressing cells is required to provide a reliable readout of drug target engagement for GPR17 antagonists.

The study lacks raw data and code availability, specifically missing the exact software versions and parameter settings for the image processing steps in Figure 2, which blocks independent verification of whether the low resolution is a display artifact or a data limitation.

The semi-quantitative pathology analysis relies on a small sample size of six to seven subjects, which is a material constraint that makes the structural claims precarious and difficult to replicate with statistical confidence.

The study's image processing pipeline cannot be verified because the raw data and scripts are not publicly available, creating a critical gap that prevents independent replication of the structural analysis.

The experimental design lacks standardized tissue preservation protocols and utilizes a small cohort with high inter-patient heterogeneity in lesion size and stage, which blocks the replication of the structural component of the recovery claim.

The primary functional outcome is derived from a sample size of n=6 or 7 per group, resulting in a 95% confidence interval wide enough to encompass the null hypothesis, which prevents definitive endorsement of the 'enhanced recovery' claim without adjusted effect sizes.

Activated microglia upregulate surface markers CD68 and MHC-II and produce specific mediators including TNF-\alpha, IL-1 \beta, IL-6, CCL2, CXCL10, reactive oxygen species, and matrix metalloproteinases.

Macrophage-like cells (MLCs) are ramified, mobile cells present at the vitreoretinal interface, and studies utilizing OCT report increased MLC number, density, and size in ocular conditions such as toxoplasmosis-related ischemic areas and active posterior uveitis.

The study enrolled 100 consecutive multiple sclerosis patients diagnosed per the 2017 McDonald criteria and 51 healthy controls at the Department of Neurology, Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, between March 2024 and October 2024.
Inclusion criteria for multiple sclerosis patients required an age between 18 and 60 years and a brain MRI with or without contrast performed within the past 12 months.

Exclusion criteria for multiple sclerosis patients included ophthalmologic or systemic disorders affecting the retina, previous history of optic neuritis, and incomplete medical release during enrollment.

Inclusion criteria for healthy controls required an age between 18 and 60 years, normal MRI findings, no history of uveitis or vitreoretinal pathology, and no personal or family history of multiple sclerosis.
Neurological evaluations for multiple sclerosis patients included the Expanded Disability Status Scale score, the Timed 25 Foot Walk, and the 9-hole Peg Test.

Spectral-domain OCT images were acquired using a Spectralis OCT device with Glaucoma Module Premium Edition software (Heidelberg Engineering, Germany) and segmented using Heidelberg Eye Explorer v2.5.1.
Macrophage-Like Cell (MLC) visualization used a Plex Elite 9000 SS-OCTA machine operating at 100 kHz, with six 6x6 mm scans centered on the fovea for each eye.
OCTA scan acceptance criteria required a signal strength of seven or higher, and the vitreoretinal interface slab was adjusted to a 3-μm depth (-7 to -10 μm from the inner limiting membrane).

Image processing utilized the "Register Virtual Stack Slices" plugin in FIJI (ImageJ) for elastic registration of six OCTA images, followed by averaging via the "AvgNoiseRmvr" plugin to enhance signal-to-noise ratio. The same transformation matrix was applied to en-face OCT slabs, which were also averaged.

Background removal and thresholding applied Fast Fourier transform (FFT) filtering and automatic brightness thresholding to highlight MLCs, with particles visually marked in red. Particle size was measured using the "Analyze Particles" filter, excluding particles smaller than 576 μm², larger than 4896 μm², or with a circularity less than 0.5.
All MLC measurements were automated using an ImageJ Macro that provided size and count data for further analysis.

Statistical analysis employed independent t-tests to compare continuous variables such as MLC parameters, ganglion cell layer (GCL) thickness, and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness between MS and control groups. A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed for categorical comparisons of MLC parameters based on treatment types and disease onset in the MS group.

Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated to explore relationships between EDSS scores and clinical measures including T1 and T2 lesions, 9-hole Peg Test times, and 25-foot walk times. Correlation analyses also evaluated associations between MLC parameters and structural metrics (GCL and RNFL) for both eyes (OD and OS) of MS patients.

The study cohort had an average time since disease onset of 6.92 years (SD=5.15 years). The distribution of disease-modifying treatments in the cohort was 65% ocrelizumab, 19% dimethyl fumarate, 8% ofatumumab, and 3% fingolimod.

The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score distribution in the MS group was 45.0% at 0.0, 16.0% at 1.0, 10.0% at 1.5, 6.0% at 2.0, 4.0% at 2.5, 4.0% at 3.0, 3.0% at 3.5, 4.0% at 4.0, 2.0% at 4.5, 1.0% at 5.0, and 4.0% at 6.0 or higher.

The mean count of T1 lesions in the cohort was 4.1 (SD=7.4) and the mean count of T2 lesions was 19.93 (SD=15.1). The correlation between EDSS score and hypointense T1 lesion count was r=0.200, and the correlation between EDSS score and T2 lesion count was r=0.365.

The average 9-hole Peg Test time was 23.13 seconds (SD=6.10) for the dominant hand and 25.06 seconds (SD=6.56) for the non-dominant hand. The average 25-foot walk time was 6.56 seconds (SD=2.13) for trial 1-in and 15.04 seconds (SD=84.19) for trial 2.
All statistical analyses were performed using Python with the pandas, scipy, and seaborn libraries, applying a significance threshold of p<0.05.

For correlation analyses between MLC parameters and MRI/clinical variables, the unit of analysis was the individual patient with MLC metrics averaged across both eyes, justified by an inter-eye correlation of r=0.635 (p<0.001) for MLC count.

Bonferroni correction adjusted the significance threshold to p<0.0083 for the six MLC-MRI correlation analyses and the six regional RNFL comparisons, and to p<0.0125 for the four regional GCL comparisons.
The study included 195 eyes from 100 patients in the multiple sclerosis group and 102 eyes from 51 patients in the control group.
The mean age was 35.08 years (SD=8.67) in the multiple sclerosis group and 35.71 years (SD=9.54) in the control group, with no significant difference in age (p=0.69).
The multiple sclerosis group comprised 91.0% relapsing-remitting phenotype, 4.0% secondary progressive phenotype, and 2.0% primary progressive phenotype.

The imaging processing pipeline involved averaging 6 consecutive optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) images after registration and averaging en-face optical coherence tomography (OCT) images after registration using the OCTA transform.
Macrophage-like cells (MLC) were identified by removing background and applying thresholding to the averaged en-face optical coherence tomography images.

The average Best Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA) in the multiple sclerosis (MS) group was 0.027 logMAR (SD=0.072), while the control group average was 0.013 logMAR (SD=0.057), with no significant difference between the groups (p=0.45).

Multiple sclerosis (MS) patients showed significantly lower ganglion cell layer (GCL) thickness in the inferior region (p=0.02) and nasal region (p=0.006) compared to controls, whereas the superior and temporal areas did not differ significantly (p=0.12 and p=0.45, respectively).
Retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) measurements showed no statistically significant differences between multiple sclerosis (MS) patients and controls across all regions analyzed.

The average microcystic lesion (MLC) parameters in the multiple sclerosis (MS) group were a count of 469.93 (SD=161.24), size of 35.79 (SD=415.86), and density of 12.86 (SD=4.72), while the control group averages were a count of 460.68 (SD=155.54), size of 6.12 (SD=0.40), and density of 12.29 (SD=4.92).

The comparison of microcystic lesion (MLC) parameters between multiple sclerosis (MS) patients and healthy controls revealed no statistically significant differences for MLC count (p=0.88), MLC size (p=0.48), or MLC density (p=0.87).

A comparison between multiple sclerosis (MS) patients with an Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score of 5 or more and healthy controls showed a significant difference in microcystic lesion (MLC) size (t=2.67, p=0.009), with MS patients with EDSS ≥ 5 exhibiting larger MLC sizes.

No significant differences were observed between multiple sclerosis (MS) patients with an EDSS score of 5 or more and healthy controls for MLC count (t=1.36, p=0.176) or MLC density (t=0.64, p=0.526).
A single data entry outlier with an MLC size of 5843 μm² was identified in one eye of a patient with EDSS<5, which inflated the mean MLC size in that subgroup.
A sensitivity analysis excluding the MLC size outlier of 5843 μm² confirmed that the pattern of results remained consistent.
The study utilized en-face optical coherence tomography (OCT) at the level of the vitreoretinal interface with a 3 μm slab for imaging.
The analysis compared macrophage-like cell (MLC) parameters between multiple sclerosis (MS) patients with Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores ≤ 5 and > 5.
The study used ANOVA to analyze MLC parameters across treatment groups, yielding MLC count (F=0.878, p=0.579), MLC size (F=0.467, p=0.937), and MLC density (F=0.693, p=0.765).
The study used ANOVA to compare MLC parameters based on onset type, yielding MLC count (F=0.807, p=0.702), MLC size (F=0.475, p=0.972), and MLC density (F=0.839, p=0.665).
The comparison between relapsing-remitting MS (n=92) and progressive MS (n=3) was underpowered, so the analysis relied on visual inspection of boxplots rather than statistical testing.

Spearman correlation was used to assess the association between MS duration and MLC characteristics, yielding MLC count (rho=0.086, p=0.401), MLC size (rho=0.145, p=0.153), and MLC density (rho=0.065, p=0.523).
Retinal microglia constitute approximately 0.2% of retinal cells and are primarily located in the Inner Plexiform Layer (IPL) and Outer Plexiform Layer (OPL).
Retinal mononuclear leukocytes (MLCs) can be visualized in vivo using adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AO-SLO) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA).
The utility of OCTA in tracking hyperreflective cells over time is demonstrated by techniques described by Castanos et al. and Uji et al.
Pichi et al. reported increased MLC density, size, and number in active posterior uveitis using OCTA.

The study identified a baseline GCL thickness threshold of less than 70 μm, which was associated with a fourfold increased likelihood of significant worsening in the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores.

The study reported specific correlation coefficients between functional metrics and EDSS scores: 9-Hole Peg Test right hand (r=0.417), 9-Hole Peg Test left hand (r=0.377), 25-foot walk trial 1 (r=0.452), and 25-foot walk trial 2 (r=0.034).

The study observed significant thinning of the GCL, particularly in the inferior and nasal regions, and identified a distinct horseshoe-shaped thinning pattern in the nasal sector (Zone M) of the macular ganglion cell and inner plexiform layer.

The cellular identity of the hyperreflective structures detected by optical coherence tomography at the vitreoretinal interface cannot be confirmed without histological validation, as these structures may include resident microglia, infiltrating macrophages, hyalocytes, or other myeloid cells.
Correlative post-mortem optical coherence tomography imaging with whole-mount immunolabeling for microglial and myeloid markers is required for biological validation of the detected structures.

The study could not obtain lesion volumes or advanced quantitative measures due to the unavailability of post-processing software at the center, restricting MRI assessment to lesion count only. Additionally, the study analyzed only brain MRI and did not include spinal cord MRI of MS patients.

The sample size of MS patients was reduced by excluding individuals with poor-quality OCT-A scans caused by nystagmus, diabetic retinopathy, or anterior segment opacities, which constrains the dataset and may introduce selection bias.
The study is a single-center investigation with a relatively small cohort, which restricts the generalizability of the results to larger, more heterogeneous populations.

Most control subjects were recruited from a neurology clinic among patients with non-specific complaints and headaches, a selection that may introduce bias due to potential neurovascular changes associated with migraines acting as confounding factors.
The study utilized a cross-sectional design, which inherently limits the ability to establish causative links between observed changes and disease progression.

OCT/OCTA imaging cannot definitively identify the cellular origin of hyperreflective particles at the vitreoretinal interface, which may include resident microglia, infiltrating macrophages, hyalocytes, or other myeloid cells. Direct histological validation requires correlative OCT imaging of post-mortem human eyes with whole-mount immunolabeling for microglial/myeloid markers (e.g., Iba-1, CD68) and vascular markers (e.g., CD31/Lectin).
For GCL and RNFL comparisons, eye-level data were used without fully accounting for within-subject correlation between fellow eyes, which may have inflated statistical significance.

The reliance on lesion counts rather than volumetric MRI measures reduced sensitivity in detecting structure-function relationships because lesion counts do not capture individual lesion size variability. Future replication requires volumetric MRI assessments including lesion volume, brain atrophy measures, and spatial lesion mapping.

The study lacks the raw data and processing scripts required to verify if the reported functional gains are genuine biological effects or pipeline artifacts, leaving only supplementary parameters available.

The specific coordinates or randomization algorithm for selecting the 3-4 histological sections per block are missing, which blocks verification of whether the anti-HLA overlap claims are representative of the whole lesion or based on cherry-picked 'best-looking' sections.

The raw data necessary to verify the stability of averaged N1-P1 amplitudes across repeated measurements is missing, making it impossible to calculate reliability coefficients or confirm that averaging both eyes does not mask subtle asymmetries in the cuprizone model.

The G-ratio calculation used a 32-image format with a default ImageJ threshold that is highly sensitive to noise, and the exact voxel size or resolution of the images is unspecified, rendering the binary thresholding parameters unverifiable.
The study analyzed the FAERS database covering the period from 2004Q1 to 2024Q4.
PML reports were identified using MedDRA Terms and manual validation.
Four algorithms (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) were jointly applied, with drugs showing signals across all four defined as high-risk.

The data analyzed in the study are publicly available from the US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) at https://www.fda.gov/drugs/questions-and-an-swers-fdas-adverse-event-reporting-system-faers/fda-adverse-event-reporting-system-faers-public-dashboard.
All data generated or analyzed during the study are included in the published article and its supplementary information files.

The study was funded by the Shanxi Provincial Department of Science and Technology, Basic Research Program (Free Exploration Category) - Youth Project under Grant No. 202403021222401 for an amount of CNY 50,000.

The study utilizes the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, which contains over 15 million reports since 1968, specifically using data spanning 2004-2024 updated to 2024Q4.

The analysis applies four complementary disproportionality algorithms: Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multi-item Gamma Poisson Shrinker (MGPS).
A drug-PML signal is defined only when all four disproportionality methods (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS) are concordant, creating a conservative signal inventory for prioritization.

The study utilized the US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, specifically records from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024, using the MedDRA Preferred Term "Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy" for PML identification.

Drug names were standardized to International Nonproprietary Names (INN), and vaccines, diagnostic agents, combination preparations, herbal medicines, and records with unclear indications were excluded from the analysis.
Indications were categorized using the MedDRA classification system into major underlying disease groups: autoimmune diseases, malignancies, organ transplantation, and other conditions.

The signal detection analysis required concordant results across four specific methods with the following thresholds: ROR > 1 with a 95% confidence interval lower bound > 1; PRR > 2 with chi-squared > 4 and N >= 3; BCPNN Information Component (IC025) > 0; and MGPS EBGM05 >= 2.

The study extracted 18,613,992 unique patient records from the FAERS database covering the period from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024 after data deduplication and multi-table integration.
Data screening resulted in 7,244 drug-PML pairings involving 298 drugs, with the complete list provided in S1 Table and the data processing flow presented in Fig 1.

The four signal detection algorithms applied were ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS, with specific thresholds defined as: PRR > 2 and chi-squared > 4 and N >= 3; BCPNN Information Component (IC025) > 0; and MGPS EBGM05 >= 2.
The study used publicly available, anonymized data from the FAERS database and complied with the FDA's FAERS data use policies.
Table 1 lists the top 30 of 72 drugs showing positive PML signals in all four detection algorithms, ranked by report numbers, with the complete list provided in S1 Table.

The statistical metrics reported in Table 1 are Reporting Odds Ratio (95% Confidence Interval), Proportional Reporting Ratio (Chi-square), Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (5th percentile of posterior distribution), and Information Component (2.5th percentile of posterior distribution).
The top 30 drugs and 30 major diseases are visualized in a heatmap in S1 Fig, where higher values indicate stronger reporting associations.
S2 Fig presents the 17 major disease categories associated with PML after consolidating the top 30 diseases.
Fig 1 illustrates the drug signal detection process for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in FAERS.
Time-to-onset (TTO) analysis was performed on the top 10 of the 72 signal-positive drugs, with TTO values visualized in Fig 5.
The pharmacovigilance analysis identified 72 drugs showing disproportionate PML reporting patterns using four independent signal detection algorithms, with results presented in Table 1 and S1 Table.

Natalizumab and rituximab had the highest PML reporting volumes with 1,848 and 1,298 reports, respectively, corresponding to Reporting Odds Ratios (ROR) of 38.08 (95% CI: 36.11-40.15) and 39.44 (95% CI: 37.13-41.9).
Mycophenolic acid and fingolimod followed with 271 reports (ROR: 12.13, 95% CI: 10.74-13.7) and 249 reports (ROR: 8.01, 95% CI: 7.06-9.09), respectively.
The Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) values for the 72 PML-associated drugs ranged from 2.91 (95% CI: 2.04-4.17) for ofatumumab to 40.42 (95% CI: 24.65-66.26) for chlorambucil.

The 72 PML-associated drugs were classified into five major pharmacological categories, with immunomodulatory drugs comprising the largest proportion, including drugs targeting lymphoid B and T cells (3,443 reports), broad-spectrum immunosuppressants (551 reports), and small molecule immunomodulators (468 reports).
Other major PML-related drug categories included hormone drugs (424 reports), cytotoxic drugs (728 reports), therapeutic drugs (103 reports), and antiviral agents (279 reports).
The study analyzed the FAERS database for drug-associated progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) reports from 2004 to 2024.
The geographic distribution map in Figure 2 was created using Datawrapper (https://app.datawrapper.de/) with a public-domain base map from Natural Earth.
The study identified 72 drugs with strong PML signals using multiple signal-detection methods applied to the FAERS database.

The study relies on the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, which is US-centric and may affect case confirmation and reporting completeness due to its reliance on MRI/cerebrospinal fluid JCV PCR for diagnosis.

The majority of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy reports in the FAERS database originate from healthcare professionals rather than patient self-reporting, which enhances the reliability of the data.

The study used four signal detection methods (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) and included only drugs identified as positive by all four methods to identify 72 PML risk drugs. The identified drugs mainly covered immunomodulators, cytotoxic drugs, biologic agents, and some novel targeted drugs.
The analysis utilized FAERS data, which is subject to reporting bias, missing data, and unmeasured confounding, meaning the findings represent disproportionality signals rather than causal inference.

FAERS data cannot effectively disentangle drug effects from baseline risk, including underlying indication, disease severity, and concomitant immunosuppression, nor can the data distinguish between therapeutic drugs and causative drugs.
The reported median time to onset (TTO) for major drugs ranges from 49 days to 1343 days, which differs from the average TTO of 29.5 months reported in Maas's study.
The study utilized the FAERS database to analyze reporting patterns of drug-associated PML.
The study identified an extended risk time window for PML ranging from 49 to 1343 days.
The study suggests that CD4+ cell counts and functional/subset features are economically feasible monitoring indicators for PML risk stratification.

Natalizumab and rituximab ranked in the top 2 by Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) in the study, but they do not directly act on CD4+ T lymphocytes, and peripheral CD4+ T lymphocyte counts increase during natalizumab treatment.
CD4+ T lymphocytes decrease during rituximab maintenance therapy, and CD4+ T counts show an upward trend when rituximab maintenance is discontinued.
In natalizumab-associated PML cases, the decrease in CD4+ T lymphocyte bioenergetics, such as intracellular ATP, may better reflect the body's immune status compared to CD4+ T cell counts.
The decrease in the frequency of central memory CD4+ T cells is more closely associated with PML occurrence than total CD4+ T cell counts.
CD4+ T lymphocyte assessment for PML risk should adopt a multidimensional strategy that includes CD4 counts, bioenergetic status (intracellular ATP concentration), and functional subsets.

Multicenter prospective cohort studies should document detailed medication histories, including monotherapy or combination regimens, cumulative doses, and sequential order, while establishing clear exposed population denominators to quantify absolute incidence risks.
Future research requires elucidating synergistic drug interactions and clarifying immunologic thresholds for JCV reactivation and host genetic susceptibility to improve risk stratification.
Developing and validating risk prediction models that integrate multidimensional indicators is crucial for translating pharmacovigilance findings into clinical practice.
Long-term monitoring approaches should integrate real-world data, international data sharing, and exploration of JCV-targeted prevention strategies to address the time-dependent nature of PML risk.

The study lacks key clinical variables such as concomitant medications, detailed underlying conditions, and treatment dosage and duration, which prevents accurate calculation of true cumulative exposure.
The FAERS spontaneous reporting system contains inherent flaws including underreporting, incomplete information, and selection bias that may distort PML signal estimation.

The geographic concentration of PML reports in European and American regions limits the global representativeness of the data due to variations in FAERS utilization and medical surveillance infrastructure.
The dataset mixes potential drug-PML associations with background PML risk from underlying indications like HIV/AIDS and lymphoma, creating confounding by indication that is difficult to disentangle.
The supporting information includes S1 Table, a list of 72 drugs with positive PML signals in all four detection algorithms ranked by case numbers, available in DOCX format.
The supporting information includes S1 Fig, a heatmap of the top 30 drugs and 30 diseases associated with PML, available in TIF format.
The supporting information includes S2 Fig, a ranking of disease categories associated with PML cases after classification merger, available in TIF format.

The statistical power for G-ratio estimates is compromised by a sample size of only 125 axons per nerve and uncorrected binary thresholding bias, which inflates variance and widens the 95% confidence interval to the point where biological recovery is indistinguishable from methodological artifact.

The walking speed data cannot distinguish a true clinical benefit from noise because the confidence interval spans the entire range from no change to moderate improvement, a limitation driven by methodological artifacts and the absence of tighter error bars or a larger sample size.

Replication of the claim that retinal markers predict future disability is blocked by the cross-sectional design, which provides only a single time-point association and lacks the follow-up data or raw OCT volumes necessary to track temporal progression.

The sampling protocol is the primary replication blocker because it provides the section count but is missing the randomization algorithm, making it impossible to establish the baseline variance for HLA overlap measurements or calculate the associated confidence intervals.

The spontaneous adverse-event analysis is currently irreproducible because the raw case counts and specific query dates are missing, preventing verification of the 72 reported PRR values or confirmation of statistical significance.
Partial replication of the spontaneous reports analysis is blocked by the absence of exact exclusion criteria and the specific software version required to run the disproportionality algorithm.
The animal and retinal imaging studies lack provided code and parameter details, making it impossible to verify specific numerical results without building the analysis pipeline from scratch.

The retinal paper’s exclusion of poor-quality scans introduces sampling bias, and the animal study relies on a specific acquisition protocol that may not translate to human tissue variability, creating gaps in generalizability for replication.
The safety analysis depends on trial design parameters that are not fully specified in the abstract, which blocks the ability to replicate the study's methodological framework.

The R scripts for the pharmacovigilance analysis are insufficient for replication because they lack the exact FAERS extract dates and exclusion criteria, which define the denominator and can shift the PRR values entirely.

The retinal imaging study cannot be verified because the specific OCT acquisition parameters and segmentation algorithms are unspecified, preventing confirmation of whether the reported ganglion cell thinning is a biological signal or a pipeline artifact.

The animal model efficacy claims are currently unverifiable due to the lack of raw data and code for the image processing pipeline, creating a critical gap that blocks independent confirmation of the biological mechanism.
The animal and imaging studies are unreproducible due to missing code and unreported acquisition parameters, preventing independent validation of the enhanced recovery findings.

Statistical re-analysis is impossible because the exact sample size (n) per group and the specific multiple-comparison corrections applied to the 72 drugs are not provided, leaving confidence intervals unverifiable.

The animal model data is statistically non-robust because the small sample size results in a 95% confidence interval wide enough to include zero, and the spontaneous reports PRR is uncorrected for the 72-drug multiplicity, rendering the signals non-interchangeable.

The human data consists of unstructured retrospective narratives rather than standardized acquisition protocols, creating a methodological gap that limits the direct relevance of the animal model findings to patient outcomes.

The statistical evidence for the drug's efficacy includes a wide confidence interval that encompasses the null, and the multiple-comparison-corrected risk estimate has not been established, preventing precise quantification of benefit or harm.

Raw OCT data and exact processing parameters must be shared upfront to eliminate pipeline variability, as the current lack of standardized acquisition protocols introduces methodological noise that obscures the signal before statistical analysis can occur.

The human reports lack the rigor to confirm whether retinal changes are a biological signal or methodological artifact, leaving the translatability of GPR17 antagonism unresolved and requiring a multi-center Phase II trial with standardized, shared imaging protocols to validate the mechanism.

A pre-registered multiple-comparison correction and a specific power calculation are required to narrow the efficacy confidence interval and define the significance threshold for safety signals, as the current spontaneous reports contain confounding that prevents clean safety validation.

* irene.knuesel@rwdtx.com #### Abstract Myelination, driven by differentiation of oligodendrocyte precursor cells, is critical for metabolic and structural support and efficient axonal signal transmission in neurons. Loss of myelin is a hallmark of multiple sclerosis and other devastating demyelinating disorders. As demyelination persists, neurons become increasingly vulnerable, leading to neurodegeneration and chronic disability. Restoring myelin through endogenous repair mechanisms offers a promising therapeutic approach to mitigate progressive neuronal loss. One key regulator of myelination is the G protein-coupled receptor 17, GPR17, whose chronic upregulation in oligodendrocyte precursor cells is commonly seen with myelin injury. In line with single-nucleus transcriptomic data showing predominant expression of GPR17 in committed oligodendrocyte precursor cells, our postmortem immunohistochemical analyses of MS patient tissue revealed a significant upregulation of GPR17 ${ }^{+} / \mathrm{BCAS} 1^{+}$oligodendrocyte precursor cells adjacent to and in demyelinated lesions. Importantly, remyelinated lesions lacked GPR17 immunoreactivity, consistent with a model in which sustained GPR17 expression is associated with demyelination and impaired oligodendrocyte precursor cell differentiation. To test the impact of pharmacological GPR17 inhibition on remyelination, we evaluated the effects of a novel, selective GPR17 antagonist in cuprizone-induced murine demyelination models. This toxin-induced approach has been widely used to study mechanisms of de- and remyelination, in the absence of the full inflammatory complexity of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis. We show that oral treatment results in robust functional recovery consistent with remyelination, as evidenced by improved spatial memory and recovery of visual evoked potential latency delays. GPR17 antagonism in promoting remyelination and highlight this G protein-coupled receptor as a promising therapeutic target for demyelinating disorders. ## Introduction Myelination, the process by which oligodendrocytes ensheathe axons with myelin, is essential for efficient nerve conduction and metabolic support of neurons in the central nervous system (CNS). Disruption of this process, or demyelination, is a defining feature of several neurological disorders, including multiple sclerosis (MS), traumatic brain injury, and ischemic or autoimmune demyelinating conditions affecting the CNS. Loss of the protective myelin sheath impairs electrical signal transmission and compromises oligodendrocyte-mediated support, ultimately contributing to the neurological deficits associated with these conditions [1]. Although the CNS possesses some capacity for endogenous myelin repair, this process is negatively influenced by numerous factors, including inflammation, axonal damage, age, and inhibitory cues in the lesion environment [2]. While certain lesions - particularly smaller or early ones - can undergo substantial or even complete remyelination [3], these repair processes are often insufficient or become progressively less effective in chronic disease settings. Persistent demyelination - often linked to central inflammatory processes - and failed repair are strongly associated with neurodegeneration and progressive functional decline across CNS disorders [4-6]. Despite recent advances in immunomodulatory therapies, including approaches targeting central inflammation (e.g., BTK inhibitors [7,8]), disease progression and disability accumulation frequently persist. These observations highlight the need for therapeutic strategies that not only modulate both peripheral and central inflammatory processes (by targeting brain myeloid cells) but also promote efficient and sustained remyelination. This is particularly relevant for patients with progressive MS, where treatment options remain largely limited to symptomatic management. Among emerging targets, G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) 17 (GPR17) has been identified as a key molecular regulator of oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination [9]. Under physiological conditions, GPR17 expression is tightly regulated and specifically expressed by a subset of early bipolar NG2 (Neural/glial antigen 2)-positive oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in the intact brain and spinal cord [10,11]. However, injury to the myelin sheath is invariably characterized by abnormal and persistent upregulation of GPR17 in OPCs, thereby impeding the final stages of oligodendrocyte maturation and maintaining OPCs in an immature state, as shown in animal models of demyelination, such as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and cuprizone- or LPC-induced demyelinating lesions [11-15]. Dysregulated GPR17 has also been described in other CNS pathologies, such as brain ischemia, traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury, Alzheimer's disease, ischemic stroke [10,12,13,16-19], as well as in human ischemic lesions [20] and demyelinating lesions [21]. Early reports suggested that GPR17 agonism may induce OPC differentiation [22]; however, more recent studies using more selective pharmacological approaches indicate that antagonism and inhibition of GPR17
functions accelerates OPC maturation and remyelination. Consequently, the prevailing view in the literature is that GPR17 signaling inhibits OPC differentiation.

Genetic and pharmacological studies support the importance of finely regulating GPR17 activity: overexpression leads to severe myelination deficits, while GPR17 knockout accelerates myelination without adverse effects [12]. Early pharmacological approaches to inhibit GPR17 functions enhanced OPC differentiation and remyelination but lacked specificity [12,23-27] leaving open the possibility that the observed effects may involve other receptor targets. In addition to lacking specificity, the mode of action of these modulators also remains to be further characterized, as the identity of the endogenous ligands for GPR17 is still under debate, a factor that has hampered the identification and characterization of selective GPR17 antagonists. Previous studies have suggested that GPR17 might be activated by cysteinyl leukotrienes [18], by purines [28,29], oxysterols such as the brain cholesterol 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol (24S-HC) [30], or most recently, by the cytokine C1q [31]. However, reproducibility efforts have failed to confirm the published data on the activity of cysteinyl leukotrienes, purines and 24S-HC [32,33], and independent validation of C1q is still lacking. Accordingly, GPR17 remains classified as an orphan receptor. Several studies revealed antagonistic activities of GPR17 targeting compounds by using the synthetic small molecule ligand, MDL-29951 demonstrating the modulation of intracellular cAMP levels, primarily via $\mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{ai}}$ signaling [27,34,35]. Notably, MDL-29,951 is the most selective and specific GPR17 agonist identified to date, and its availability has enabled the identification and characterization of GPR17 antagonists. MDL-29951 was also included in this study, revealing a competitive antagonism of RWT020016.

In early efforts to study GPR17 functions, non-selective GPR17 antagonists such as Pranlukast and Montelukast were used, providing preliminary insights into its role in remyelination. However, their lack of selectivity and specificity limited the ability to directly attribute observed effects to GPR17 antagonism [24,26,27,36]. Nevertheless, these preclinical studies highlighted the therapeutic potential of promoting remyelination, although translating such strategies to clinical benefit has remained challenging. One major challenge is the direct translation of preclinical findings in animal models to complex neurological diseases in humans. While toxin-induced demyelination models, such as the cuprizone paradigm, are well suited to study mechanisms of de- and remyelination in a controlled setting, they do not fully recapitulate the inflammatory and heterogeneous pathology of multiple sclerosis, which must be considered when translating preclinical findings to human disease.

Early clinical trials have demonstrated that remyelination in humans is possible [37,38], yet achieving consistent and clinically meaningful outcomes has proven difficult. In addition to methodological challenges, such as selecting sensitive imaging and biomarker endpoints, past trials have encountered limitations including off-target side effects (e.g., fatigue and insomnia with histamine H3 antagonists such as Clemastine and GSK239512) [39], as well as metabolic disturbances with Bexarotene [40]. Questions have also been raised regarding trial design, including suitability of comparators (e.g., interferon-beta in anti-LINGO-1 trials), which may not have adequately controlled the inflammatory processes. Furthermore, therapeutic modalities involving antibodies (e.g., Elezanumab targeting RGMa) may have been limited by insufficient brain exposure, potentially reducing their efficacy in promoting remyelination [41,42]. While these challenges need to be addressed in future clinical trials, targeting selectively and specifically GPR17 offers a promising therapeutic approach as it shows an almost exclusive expression in the CNS, in OPCs.

In the current study, we investigated a novel, highly potent and selective small molecule GPR17 antagonist RWT020016. This compound was designed to overcome the shortcomings of earlier pharmacological agents by directly promoting endogenous OPC maturation. This study evaluated the selective GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 for its ability to promote OPC differentiation by releasing the injury-induced block at the committed OPC (COP) stage, expected to facilitate remyelination in a pathological context where GPR17 is dysregulated. GPR17 expression was characterized in postmortem human brain and optic nerve tissue, complemented by a bioinformatics approach using single-nucleus RNA sequencing data. In addition, efficacy was examined in toxin-induced demyelination mouse models, focusing on both acute and chronic cuprizone treatment effects, using functional and behavioral readouts - including visual evoked
potentials (VEPs) and a Y-maze test assessing spatial working memory - as well as structural readouts, including quantification of myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum and assessment of myelin ultrastructure via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in the optic nerve. These findings support the potential of GPR17 antagonism as a transformative therapy for demyelinating diseases. ## Methods ## Single nucleus transcriptome meta-analysis To generate a comprehensive overview of oligodendrocyte maturation, five public single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets spanning a range of diseases and subject ages were collected [5,43-46]. Raw count matrices were obtained from their respective repositories, yielding a total of 214,567 nuclei across all dataset. A consistent quality control (QC) and preprocessing pipeline was applied across datasets using the Seurat R package (version 3.1) [47-49] to ensure comparability and minimize technical variability. Cells were filtered based on standard QC metrics, excluding low-quality nuclei characterized by low gene counts or high mitochondrial transcript content, thereby reducing technical noise and potential batch-specific artifacts. To account for dataset heterogeneity and mitigate batch effects arising from differences in sample origin, sequencing platform, or processing pipelines, datasets were integrated using the Seurat integration workflow. This approach aligns shared biological features across datasets while preserving biologically meaningful variation. Following integration, dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis (PCA), with the number of variable features set to 7,500 and 75 principal components retained for downstream analysis. Cells were then embedded using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) based on the integrated PCA space. Clustering was performed using a graph-based approach (FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions), with resolution parameters selected to achieve biologically meaningful separation of major cell populations while avoiding overclustering. Cell-type annotation was initially guided by author-provided labels when available and further refined using canonical marker genes for oligodendrocyte lineage populations, including OPCs, committed oligodendrocyte precursors (COPs), and mature oligodendrocytes. Cells belonging to the oligodendrocyte lineage were subsequently subsetted, and integration, dimensionality reduction, and clustering steps were repeated to refine the representation of oligodendrocyte differentiation, resulting in a final dataset of 71,623 cells. Marker genes for each cluster were identified using Seurat's FindAllMarkers function with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Differential expression analyses between selected clusters (e.g., OPC versus COP populations) were performed using FindMarkers with the same statistical framework.

Differences were considered statistically significant at $p<0.05$. ## Results ## GPR17 expression in committed oligodendrocyte precursors is conserved in human brain Single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis of oligodendrocyte lineage cells, combined from five human brain studies, was performed with a special emphasis on markers of oligodendrocyte maturation [5,43-46]. A total of 214,567 cells were included in the analysis, with a population of 71,623 cells of the oligodendrocyte lineage. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plots were used to visualize major CNS cell populations (S1A-B Fig), including astrocytes, microg-lia, neurons, oligodendrocytes and OPCs. Cluster identities were validated using canonical marker genes for microglia (FYB1, C3, S1C-D Fig), astrocytes (AQP4, GJA1, S1E-F Fig), oligodendrocytes (MOBP, MBP, S1G-H Fig), neurons (GRIN1, GAD2, SLC17A7, S1I-K Fig), and endothelial cells (CLDN5, S1L Fig). Lineage progression from OPCs to NFOLs was confirmed by the expression of stage-specific markers (SOX6, BMP4, TNS3, TCF7L2, CASR, FYN, ITPR2, S1O-V Fig). The analysis revealed that GPR17 expression was largely restricted to the oligodendrocyte lineage, with no detectable transcripts in other major CNS cell types, including astrocytes, microglia, neurons, or endothelial cells (S1 Fig). Sample-based integration of non-neuronal cells minimized dataset- and sample-specific variation, enabling clear
delineation of the rare and transient population of committed oligodendrocyte precursors (COPs). These COPs were characterized by relatively higher GPR17 expression compared to OPCs, alongside the presence of additional markers associated with early differentiation stages, including FYN kinase and myelin-related genes such as PLP1 and MBP [62]. Other COP-associated markers (e.g., SOX6, TNS3, FYN) showed enrichment but were not exclusively restricted to this population (S1O, R, U Fig). As illustrated in the UMAP projection (Fig 1B), GPR17 expression appeared to peak within the COP population and decline as cells transitioned toward myelin-forming and mature oligodendrocytes (S1Q Fig). While these observations are primarily descriptive, they consistently support an enrichment of GPR17 expression at the COP stage relative to adjacent maturation states. A smaller subset of OPCs also exhibited detectable GPR17 expression, albeit at lower levels. Together, these findings highlight a transient yet prominent association of GPR17 expression with the COP maturation stage in the human brain.

After cuprizone administration, animals were returned to normal placebo pellets to allow spontaneous remyelination for 1 week and 5 weeks respectively. Compound treatment was initiated two days prior to cuprizone withdrawal to ensure sufficient compound concentration in the brain to initiate remyelination (Fig 3 A-B). To evaluate functional recovery and remyelination following cuprizone-induced demyelination, we assessed visual evoked potential (VEP) latency and amplitude in both the acute and the chronic model. In clinical practice, this method is used to assess the functional integrity of the visual pathways, particularly in the context of demyelinating disease, such as MS. Demyelination slows the conduction of action potentials, which is reflected as a prolongation of VEP latency, while a reduction in amplitude may indicate axonal injury or sustained demyelination [64]. VEPs were assessed at baseline, at the end of the demyelination phase (at week 6 for acute and at week 12 for chronic) and at the end of the remyelination phase (at week 7 for acute and at week 17 for chronic). At the end of the demyelination phase, both models showed a significant increase in VEP latency ( $p<0.0001$ vs. control for acute; $p<0.0001$ vs. control for chronic, Fig 3 C-D), while VEP amplitudes remained comparable to those of control mice, indicating the absence of axonal loss in either model (data not shown), in line with previous findings [65].

In addition, the impact of demyelination on axonal signal conduction can manifest in deficits in cognitive performance. Cognitive processing speed and episodic memory, including short-term working memory, are the most frequently affected cognitive domains in patients with MS [66]. At week 6, no significant difference was observed in the total arm entries between control and cuprizone-treated mice (Fig 3 E) indicating that cuprizone did not affect general locomotor activity. However, at week 12, cuprizone-treated mice showed a significant increase in total arm entries compared with controls ( $p<0.0001$ vs. control, Fig 3 F), indicating hyperactivity or altered exploratory behavior following chronic cuprizone treatment. Furthermore, in both models, cuprizone-treated mice showed a reduction in spontaneous alternation compared with control mice, indicative of impaired working memory due to demyelination (Fig 3 G-H).
